Given the slowing demand for electric vehicles in the U.S., it comes as no surprise that Honda canceled three EVs planned for North America. The brand’s first mass-market EV in the region, the Prologue, is also being discontinued after just over two years on the market. Among the canceled models was the 0 SUV, which was intended to rival the Tesla Model Y. However, a newly granted U.S. design patent appears to bring the canceled SUV back to life, at least on paper.

The patent, first spotted by CarMoses, includes several drawings depicting what appears to be the 0 SUV prototype from different angles. The prototype was unveiled at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, alongside the 0 Saloon prototype. Both were later canceled, along with the Acura RSX, completing the trio of EVs that never made it to production.

Looking at the patent drawings, the side profile closely matches that of the 0 SUV prototype, particularly the rear quarter window between the C- and D-pillars. This design element is absent from the 0 Alpha, the smallest model unveiled in the 0 Series lineup. The 0 Alpha also features rear door handles integrated into the C-pillars, similar to the Honda HR-V and Toyota C-HR, helping create a coupe-like appearance. In contrast, the patent drawings show conventionally positioned door handles, matching those of the 0 SUV prototype.

The pixel-like headlights of the 0 SUV prototype also appear to be reflected in the patent drawings. Another matching design element is the front bumper, which features a prominent horizontal black trim piece and a sportier appearance than the one on the 0 Alpha.

Apart from those details, the patent could resemble either the 0 SUV or 0 Alpha prototype. Both share a similar boxy shape with a sloping roofline and pronounced wheel arches. Mentioning the 0 Alpha here is relevant, given that Honda hasn’t canceled it. However, it is primarily intended for Japan and India.

But again, these comparisons are based on visual cues only, so nothing is confirmed. Automakers often patent vehicle designs to protect their styling from competitors or preserve them for future use. After all, quirky, boxy shapes seem to be the go-to these days, as seen with the latest generations of the Hyundai Santa Fe and Lexus GX.

Honda’s focus in North America is now shifting toward hybrids, including the next-generation CR-V Hybrid, whose production was reportedly delayed by about three months to April 2027. The automaker plans to introduce 15 next-gen hybrid models globally by 2030, primarily targeting North America.

#4574. Tested: 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive Is in a Neue Klasse of Its Own

With strong performance and class-leading range, the sedan makes a compelling argument for going electric. But will potential buyers care?

First came the EVs that looked very obviously like electric cars, with wacky designs showing off their futuristic powertrains. Then there was a generation that hid EV powertrains under bodywork shared with combustion-powered models. And now we are encountering a new strain, EVs that look almost identical to regular siblings but sit on radically different underpinnings. And the BMW i3 is the best example yet of this new genre. From the outside, it looks almost indistinguishable from the gasoline-powered G50 3-series, but every exterior panel is different, and it sits on a completely different architecture, BMW’s Neue Klasse EV platform. The distinction is great enough that it even gets its own BMW model code—this is the NA0.

The Neue Klasse underpinnings mean the i3 shares its powertrain with the iX3 SUV that was launched ahead of it. The closeness of the relationship is shown by the 114.1-inch wheelbase shared by both models, primarily dictated by the use of the same battery pack.

The first version of the electric sedan to reach the U.S. will be the i3 50 xDrive, which uses a pair of electric motors, one powering each axle, to deliver a combined system output of 463 horsepower and 476 lb-ft of torque. The 800-volt battery stores 108.7 kWh of usable energy, and the i3’s lower profile and more slippery shape mean it will boast an EPA range of up to 468 miles. It also supports DC fast-charging at rates of up to 400 kW, making it theoretically possible to take the battery from a 10 percent to 80 percent state of charge in as little as 21 minutes. Providing you can hook it up to a sufficiently juicy plug, of course.

Other versions will follow, including an M60 version that will share the more potent powertrain of the iX3 M60 xDrive, making over 600 horsepower. Beyond that there is the fully electric M3 to look forward to, but for now we’ll concentrate on the meat-and-potatoes 50 xDrive.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Powertrain: dual electric motors, all-wheel drive

EPA Range: <468 miles (depending on wheels and tires)

Driving the i3 back-to-back with its 3-series doppelgänger, the new M350 xDrive, gave a fascinating insight into BMW’s priorities. Because it’s fair to say, when it comes to driving dynamics, that the EV has much more in common with the iX3 than it does with its combustion sibling. The M350 feels largely familiar, essentially a retuned and more powerful version of the previous-generation M340i xDrive. The i3 is breaking new ground for a BMW sedan. And yes, that comparison includes the old i4, which was—beneath its low-roofed bodywork—essentially an electric version of the last 3-series.

BMW has spent big on its Neue Klasse platform, and the i3 50 drove with a sense of oneness and harmony that proved the scale of the colossal engineering effort spent on integrating its different systems and making them play nice together. This was obvious in the smoothness of the powertrain, the poise of the chassis, and the exceptional refinement. This is clearly the new 3-branded model on which the big bucks have been spent.

Before I heap too much praise, I need to make an important proviso: The i3 50 is not, intrinsically, an exciting car. It is capable of delivering adrenaline spikes through quantities of longitudinal and lateral g-forces, but it completely lacks the rowdy character common to the BMWs that enthusiasts really love. Driving the i3 after experiencing the M350’s snarling engine and more aggressive suspension tune made the EV feel a little like a wallflower.

But that first impression was unfair. There’s a subtlety to the way the i3 50 does pretty much everything. No part of the experience really stands out, but that’s because everything is being done just so, and cruising refinement is almost spookily good. There is still a speaker-delivered soundtrack to try to introduce some excitement to proceedings, and it was too loud and intrusive in Sport mode. But this is switchable, and near silence suits the i3 much better.

By the increasingly deranged standards of the sharp end of the EV segment, performance is warm rather than outright hot: BMW claims a 4.5-second 0–60, which is actually 0.6 second slower than the M350. But it felt plenty keen behind the wheel, with the fractional difference in acceleration more than compensated for by not needing to change gears. Like the best EVs, the i3 has the ability to almost teleport itself into gaps and make passing moves at minimal notice. And while the rate of acceleration started to noticeably slacken over 85 mph, it still feels plenty rapid. Ultimately, BMW says, it will reach a 124-mph speed limiter.

Slowing impressed more than going, thanks to the completely seamless switching between regenerative and friction braking, the exceptionally finely tuned one-pedal mode, and also the Soft Stop feature—called “chauffeur stop” by other automakers—which brings the i3 to a genuinely imperceptible halt by easing braking progressively in the final few feet in its one-pedal mode. In addition to switchable regen levels, there is also an adaptive function that automatically increases this when the vehicle is approaching junctions or has other reasons to slow down, and it worked delicately enough to be hardly noticeable. The enhanced cruise control also worked well on different types of road, with the Highway Assistant function giving hands-off freeway functionality.

Most comments are exactly the same as those for the new 3-series. Despite their different underlying architectures, the 3-series and the i3 have what are almost identical cabins. The only obvious changes are that the EV doesn’t have gearchange paddles behind its steering wheel, a rev counter, or a start button; as long as the key is detected within the car, you just select a gear and go. Beyond that, the biggest difference I noticed was that the i3’s lowest seat position was higher than the M350’s, which was a mild frustration. Other comments regarding the sometimes fiddly inputs of the user interface are exactly the same for both cars.

The Neue Klasse cabin architecture was clearly designed with EVs higher on the priority list than combustion models. The Panoramic Vision projected dash display is better suited for delivering the minimal messages required the i3, losing the frustration of the M350’s inadequate rev counter and vestigial fuel gauge. There is still too much display real estate for the information that needs to be delivered, but the reconfigurable slots mean buyers will be able to make their own choices about what to look at, including images of some of BMW’s Art Cars.

I didn’t get the chance to test either the peak charging speed or the veracity of the impressive range claim. That will happen when Road & Track gets more time with a car in the States.

Potential buyers face two big questions. The first, if they are set on making the slightly eccentric choice of a compact EV sedan, is whether the i3 represents the best of the breed. Of the limited pool, the Mercedes C-class Electric, also set to reach the U.S. next year, is probably the closest alternative. But the Tesla Model 3 Performance is also a pretty close match in terms of power output, and it’s slightly less expensive, although it doesn’t get close to the BMW’s EPA range or dynamic polish.

But here’s a trickier question: Does this buyer really want an EV? For anyone determined to take the electric path, the i3 50 xDrive makes a great case for itself, one that will be strengthened as the model range fills out with other variants. But for those who prefer a more traditional take on the small BMW sedan or are sitting on the fence, the new 3-series provides what is still a compelling reason to say no. By empirical standards, the i3 is a better car, but it is not a more exciting one.

The chance to put pictures of some of BMW’s famous Art Cars onto the panoramic gauge cluster might feel like whimsy in a less serious car, but the i3 gets a pass given how relentlessly well it does pretty much everything else. As in other models with the new Panoramic Vision system, you can choose among five, including David Hockney’s superb BMW 850 CSi, seen here.

#4573. How We’d Spec It: 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500

If you think one of our four staffers wants to spend over $60K on a new truck, you’d be dead wrong.

The 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500 is kind of a big deal. That’s because in America, full-size pickup trucks are one of the most popular things to own, especially when they wear a Ford, GMC, Ram, or Chevy logo. And if you know anything about half-ton trucks, you know that General Motors just introduced new generations of the Sierra 1500 and Silverado 1500. Both are now available to order, and you can spec your ideal version on their respective brand’s consumer sites. Since Chevy’s truck is the more popular one, we set four staffers loose on the configurator and tasked them with creating their ideal version. The trim levels they chose might surprise you.

The street truck: A movement past its prime or just getting started? I’m an optimist, and I choose to believe the latter. My Gen X ancestors refined this style of vehicle long ago during the Dubya administration with factory trucks such as the Toyota Tacoma X-Runner, second-generation Ford F-150 SVT Lightning, and of course, the Dodge Ram SRT-10. I am determined to keep the arts alive with my built-to-spec 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 for sale near 94112

Regular cab, standard bed, two-wheel drive, and a sick paint job. Apex Red, to be exact, for no additional cost. This is a WT-trim Silverado with as few options as I can manage. To be clear, the goal of this build is to prepare for aftermarket modifications. It’s unfortunate that I’m stuck with the 2.7-liter turbo four, but my imagination is running rampant, and I see an LT6 flat-plane-crank V-8 from the Corvette Z06 in my engine bay’s future. I’m keeping the wheels and tires standard to inevitably replace later; however, I will be switching from the Evotex seats to cloth, as the latter fabric is a far superior interior material. Even better than leather—argue with me in the comments. None of the available options excite me for this build; I’m trying to keep the price somewhat reasonable, but I’m a sucker for cosmetic details, so I’ve selected the black bowtie emblem for $325. From the factory, my Silverado rings up at $41,720, but there’s more coming.

The aftermarket hasn’t quite arrived for the ‘27 Silverado 1500, but I think it’s safe to say when it does, prices will look somewhat similar to what’s available for the current 2026 models. I found a lowering kit for 2019–2026 Silverados from McGaughy’s Suspension Parts. It drops the front by 2.5 inches and the rear by 4 inches for $1380. I’m sitting here thinking about what wheels would work on a street truck, and Mickey Thompson crossed my mind. I like the simple look of the cast aluminum MT Open 5, and I’m going for the 20-inch set, which cost $285.99 per wheel (so $1143.96 for all four). Next, I think it’d be pretty dumb to put all-terrain tires on a lowered truck, so it’s a good thing Nitto makes a tire for just this case. It’s called the NT420V, and it’s designed to accommodate large-diameter wheels. The Mickey Thompsons I chose are 9 inches wide, so I’m going with 265/45R-20 tires, which will likely stretch the rubber a bit. A set of four costs $924 before taxes. That’s wheels, tires, and suspension done, which is all I would need to do, to be honest. Window tint? Sure, I’d get a quote on that, but that’s a later issue. All that’s left is to drop that LT6 in the bay. Anyone have a Z06 they’d like to donate? Not including the engine swap, that’s $45,167.96 for my perfect Silverado 1500.–Carter Fry

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 for sale near 94112

Everyone seems to love a four-door truck you can pack your whole family or group of friends in and hit the boulevard or interstate. But what if you want a good reason to limit your passenger space to no more than three people? A regular-cab pickup provides the perfect excuse, and I’m pumped that Chevy still sells this configuration with its new half-ton Silverado. The base Work Truck (WT) starts at $41,395, but that price can climb considerably higher with options, as you can see from my ideal spec.

A rear-drive truck is great fun unless you live in a four-season region like my home state of Michigan. Even with a set of winter tires, an unladen rear axle will struggle for traction on slippery streets, so I added the $4600 four-wheel-drive system. Dropping another $970 got me the 4x4-specific Work Truck package, which includes a useful automatic mode for the two-speed transfer case as well as all-terrain tires, underbody skid plates, and hill-descent control. I paired that with the $395 automatic locking rear diff to give my stout little truck some extra off-road cred.

One of the cool things about the new Chevy Silverado is that even the cheapest version gets the fully digital gauge cluster and large 16.3-inch infotainment touchscreen. I’m also a big fan of bench seats, and a 40/20/40 layout is standard on the WT. I spec’d mine with cloth upholstery, and while the all-black interior looks undeniably drab, I don’t have a choice in the matter. At least it matches the paint job. I stuck with the steel wheels because I’ll definitely bolt on an aftermarket set.

While they’re hard to see in the photos, I added several options to make my Work Truck feel like it was built post-1985. I scored a power-adjustable driver’s seat with 10 settings, including lumbar, by opting for the $515 Power package. I also got a leather-wrapped steering wheel for just $75, and the heated version added $150. The Assisted Driving package includes a 360-degree camera system and perimeter lighting for $545, and the $1175 WT Convenience package finished out my options list with the following upgrades: anti-theft system, deep tinted glass, remote start, 120-volt outlets inside and in the cargo bed, and a tailgate that’s somehow easier to lift. All told, my 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500 WT came to $49,920.–Eric Stafford

While the luxurious High Country and aggressive ZR2 were tempting, I decided to keep my Silverado practical and relatively affordable. I paired the crew cab and short bed with the LT trim. The turbocharged 2.7-liter four-cylinder comes standard with rear-wheel drive and starts at $53,195. Every LT includes a power-sliding rear window, heated seats, and adaptive cruise control too.

The White Sands paint was a no-cost option, and I stuck with the standard 18-inch wheels, both to save some dough and because the tires’ extra sidewall will benefit ride quality. Inside, I upgraded to the black-and-tan upholstery for a bit of visual pop, which required adding the Comfort and Convenience package for $2290. It swaps the front bench seat for two buckets and adds an eight-speaker Bose stereo, front USB ports, a 120-volt power outlet, wireless phone charging, and a center console that can fold out into a workspace.

There were other features I would have wanted a la carte, such as a head-up display, ventilated front seats, and a rear camera mirror, but they were only available as part of the $5275 Silverado Premium Package, so I skipped it. I can survive without those niceties. The only other item I threw in was a set of front and rear all-weather floor mats, bringing my total to $55,770.–Caleb Miller

Unless we’re talking about a ZR2 Bison or a truck with equally high performance, the idea of spending more than $80,000 on a pickup conjures a feeling in my gut that I’d generally associate with the fallout from eating bad fish.

That’s why I opted for the much more budget-friendly Work Truck (WT). That said, I know truck buying is not the time for penny-pinching, so I was happy to add the $350 17-inch silver wheels to drop the look of the standard steelies. I was also happy to spend the roughly $9000 required to upgrade from the regular cab to the crew cab and standard bed—if you’re going to buy a half-ton pickup, you may as well buy one with tons of space, right?

As much as I’d rather spend my time in the considerably nicer High Country trim, when the heated steering wheel is a $150 option, heated side mirrors are $100, and the WT Convenience package that adds remote start, extra 120-volt connections, an EZ-lift tailgate, and a tailgate camera angle is just $1175, I’ve got all the luxury I need. Still, for all my posturing, I’m a sucker for a V-8, and the 5.7 in the new Silverado is a lovely mill. It pulls hard, sounds great, and has the added benefit of increasing maximum towing to 16,100 pounds, so I’m happy to spend the necessary $2690 to replace the standard turbo four. Altogether, my Silverado came to $57,415. It’s certainly not cheap, but it’s also not nearly as expensive as modern pickups can get. –Jack Fitzgerald

#4572. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4571. Repair Shop Quoted a Man $1,200 to Replace a $150 Muffler He Didn't Need

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

A “high-profile” repair shop quoted a man $1,264.40 to replace a muffler, when all he needed was a $17 exhaust gasket.

Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol Ditches Roof and Luxury for Serious Off-Roading

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

Inside Doug DeMuro's Secret Underground Car Garage

McLaren's Manual V8 McL 6GT Makes Its Public Debut in Las Vegas

For a thousand bucks, you could get a lot of work done on your car, and a repair shop in Vermont reviewed a quote from a “high-profile” repair shop that could have cost a customer nearly ten times the cost of the part itself.

A video was posted on TikTok by mainly_mechanics (@mainly_mechanics) detailing a quote from another shop that appears to have overcharged a customer for a part that he didn’t even need.

It seems rather outrageous that a stock replacement muffler would cost over a thousand dollars to purchase. Apparently, it doesn’t cost that much, according to mainly_mechanics, while tagging TJ’s Auto Repair in Burlington, Vermont. In this video, he showed the quote that the other shop gave his customer.

The breakdown of the muffler replacement was as follows: $1,082 for the replacement muffler assembly, $17 for the gasket, and $4.24 for the nuts and bolts; then the rest is for about 48 minutes of labor, which totals $1,264.40. On the same quote was a note from the shop saying that the vehicle’s current muffler assembly “is rusted and leaks; will fail VSI (a.k.a. Vermont State Inspection).” The note is a bit of a scare tactic, which would otherwise render the car illegal to drive and register in Vermont.

The thing is, Vermont accepts repair jobs as long as the repair is as good as, or if not better than, OEM. A complete muffler replacement might not have been necessary in the first place if the muffler was damaged.

According to mainly_mechanics, the cost of a new muffler, if it were purchased by him as a business, would come out to $157 dollars. If the customer would like to purchase the part himself, the amount would go up by about ten bucks, and if the customer were to get the part through a retailer, it would total almost $300. Nowhere in any of mainly_mechanic’s quotes did they get even remotely close to $1,200, even after accounting for labor.

Including parts and labor, plus the $17 gasket, the $4.24 set of nuts and bolts, and the $159.99 for 48 minutes of labor, we get $348.23. That’s about a third of the price that the other shop would have charged the customer. The thing is, mainly_mechanics didn’t state this number themselves because, based on their assessment of the vehicle, the customer didn’t even need to buy a new muffler.

The main issue here isn’t just the price of the part, but the fact that the car didn’t even need it in the first place. Later in the video, mainly_mechanics then showed us the muffler that was supposed to be replaced. It was determined that the exhaust gasket and the bolts were the only things that needed replacing, as the leaks were coming from there.

Moving to the back of the car, there were no such leaks to speak of. There was some surface rust, but not enough that would punch a hole through the body of the muffler or any of the connecting pipes. If the customer went ahead and spent on just the gasket and the bolts, minus the labor, he would have come out about $21 bucks poorer, then maybe about a hundred bucks in labor for the simpler job, and the total might come out to around $150 more or less.

In defense of this “high-profile” shop, maybe the customer was given an initial diagnosis without a thorough underchassis inspection. Based on the available information on the post, it could have been an initial quote, which was there to give the customer an idea of just how expensive it could get. Now, if this shop actually conducted the inspection and then quoted the customer its price for the muffler replacement, then there’s a problem.

The car in question is also a mystery. There was no mention of a year, make, or model of the car, which doesn’t give us a clear picture of what prices to expect for replacement parts. With a list price of $284, though, according to mainly_mechanics, it also calls into question where the part is coming from, whether it’s from an OEM or aftermarket replacement manufacturer.

Mainly_mechanics didn’t go into detail about where he sourced the $157 replacement from. You could speculate that the part was an aftermarket OEM replacement, while the part that the “high-profile” shop was selling was from the manufacturer, which could explain the high cost, somewhat (not really). Aftermarket or third-party replacement parts are designed to deliver similar performance to the OEM part that they replace, though there is a difference in price and quality, which is noted by the Federal Trade Commission.

Still, a $900-plus profit does sound criminal, but a quote is not a charge. I’d make an issue if that “high-profile” shop ended up charging the customer, but it’s a good thing he managed to shop around before bringing out his wallet. I guess the lesson here is to be aware of your vehicle’s issue and make sure that the shop handling it does its due diligence by properly inspecting your vehicle and showing you what’s wrong with it before any quote is given.

#4570. 2027 BMW 3-Series Drive: Not Just Different but Better

You’re all thinking it. This Neue Klasse BMW 3-series is launching at the same time as the battery-powered i3, so the regular 3-series has to be compromised in some way to accommodate the all-electric version. No, it’s nothing like the 430i versus i4 situation. In that case, the platform was engineered to make it possible to fit either powertrain. With the Neue Klasse era, gas and EV each have their own platform. They’re even built at different plants. The 2027 BMW 3-series is assembled in Dingolfing, Germany, while the i3 is made in Munich.

We can therefore look at the combustion-powered 3-series primarily on its own merits. The 2027 BMW M350 xDrive and the entry-level 330 (in rear-wheel drive or xDrive all-wheel-drive configurations), which no longer have a trailing “i” attached because that’s now a prefix that means something else, can be directly compared with the outgoing M340i xDrive and 330i.

See all results for new 2027 BMW 3-series for sale near 02108

The new generation brings some minor growth: a touch more wheelbase (up 0.4 inch to 112.6), a bit more length (up 1.7 inches to 187.6), and a smidgen wider (up 0.9 inch to 72.8). It’s somewhat taller, too, but the 0.6-inch increase to 57.3 inches is mostly due to the inch-taller rolling diameter of the new standard 19- and optional 20-inch tires. A bit more concerning is the roughly 200-pound weight gain, which we estimate should put the M350 at close to 4200 pounds.

The new car looks strikingly different, as the brand’s Neue Klasse styling is in full effect. It starts with a forward-leaning grille that is spread across the front end in a low smirk, the twin kidneys stretched to credulity and blending with the headlights at the margins. It still has the long-hood proportions necessary to accommodate an inline-six-cylinder engine, with squared-off flanks that look fairly attractive in person. The hood is a bit higher and flatter, though. As before, the cabin is set rearward and blends neatly into a stubby trunk that can accommodate 16 cubic feet of goods, only a bit less than before. On the M350, the badging is a bit misleading, as the “M3” is almost twice the size of the “50.”

The two engines in the 3-series both use the Miller cycle to shorten intake-valve opening time when necessary for the optimum air-fuel ratio. They also use switchable exhaust valves to reduce engine braking so there’s more regen to be harvested by the 48-volt hybrid-assist system. In the 330, that adds up to the same 255 horsepower and 295 pound-feet we’ve seen before, but that’s still impressive because it meets Europe’s stricter emissions standards. The M350, on the other hand, gets a whole lot more. It features reshaped intake ports and combustion chambers, as well as revisions to camshaft timing, fuel injection, and exhaust-gas routing. But the new, larger turbo is the party piece that pumps up the output to 437 horses instead of the M340i’s 386. BMW says that adds up to a tenth of a second or two quicker to 60 mph (a 2023 M340i xDrive hit that mark in 3.7 seconds in our testing).

See all results for new 2027 BMW 3-series for sale near 02108

As for the chassis, there is a slightly wider front subframe, which accounts for much of the increase in front track. BMW has tweaked the links of the dual-link strut front suspension a bit, such that the caster angle is higher, and the static negative camber is down a smidge. These changes were made to improve on-center feel and effort buildup, and all we can say is “Yes, please!” Sure, at very slow parking-lot speeds the steering’s electrically assisted boost is readily apparent, but as speed builds, that quickly fades away, and a pure mechanical feel takes over. The response becomes direct and accurate, and we think BMW nailed it this time.

All 3-series models have stiffer anti-roll bar mounts, so there’s less flex, and the bar can do its work more efficiently. The rear bushings have also been optimized for their passive steering characteristics, so there’s just enough toe-in to feel secure, but not so much that the car’s playfulness is drained away. Also, the base dampers are called “lift-related” because they now have a hydraulic rebound stop instead of a rebound spring.

Unfortunately, BMW didn’t have any 330 models for us to sample. Instead, we drove the M350 xDrive on the wonderful roads of southern France; it comes standard with things that are optional on the 330. This includes the Adaptive M suspension, variable sport steering, an M Sport differential, and a strut tower brace.

The Adaptive M suspension has been retuned to be more dynamic (the Germans love that word; see also “dynamism”) while also being more comfortable. The relationship between rebound and compression damping is certainly improved, and that goes a long way toward comfort. But the roads weren’t beat up like they often are back home, so the jury is still out. BMW also monkeyed with the M Sport differential and the xDrive torque-split characteristics, so the car can now help you better hold your line even if you overcook a corner. We tried it out by entering a bend a touch hot, expecting understeer, but the M350 just didn’t seem to care.

Inside, the front seats are supremely comfortable, and the rears are particularly soft. There was headroom in abundance in our car with its panoramic glass roof, but kneeroom was kind of tight for our 6-foot-2-inch tester to sit behind himself. That said, it’s certainly bigger and better back here than in the M340i. There’s a wonderful Harman/Kardon stereo too, which can play Dolby Atmos tracks on a three-dimensional soundstage. This all comes across as fantastic, but there is an elephant in the room, and it’s called Neue Klasse.

The Neue Klasse newness is most evident in the driver interface. Most of it is great, from the angled 17.9-inch touchscreen to the Panoramic Vision instrument displays projected on a blacked-out strip that spans the entire base of the windshield. But there are quirks, from the odd shape and arrangement of the spokes on the steering wheel to the presence of a (thankfully optional) head-up display. Who needs a head-up display when you have Panoramic Vision? The former projects map turn data, which you can see elsewhere, on the windshield right on top of the traffic you’re supposed to be watching. And the widgets to the right, in front of the passengers, are frankly distracting. Better to turn them off and stick with the ones directly in front of you, which, thankfully, you can do. Also, a dearth of fixed buttons makes adjusting many things, including the air vents, a trip through touchscreen submenu hell.

That said, this is a Software Defined Vehicle (SDV), so many things you want are coming soon or will be enhanced through over-the-air updates. Chief among them is something called Drift Moment, which will be pushed out to all M350 xDrive customers as soon as it passes muster. This feature diverts all power to the rear wheels with the DSC off, to basically put the car in drift mode. When it arrives, the activation button will appear alongside the already present Launch Control mode, which itself is dead simple to use. Another cool feature of this SDV is the hands-free driving mode called Highway Assistant, which works on limited-access highways at speeds up to 85 mph. It also supports automated entry-to-exit guidance and will even perform automatic lane changes when they’re confirmed by a glance in the relevant rearview mirror.

All versions of the new 3-series, and the related-but-unrelated new i3, will be released at the same time near the end of the first quarter of 2027. Prices range from $51,250 for a 330 to $67,250 for an M350 xDrive. If you like the look of the 2027 BMW 3-series in all its Neue Klasse glory, then we feel confident that you’ll fall in love with the way it drives.

#4569. Tested: 2027 Audi Q9 Brings Big Space and Big Tech

The extra-large Q9 fills an obvious gap in Audi’s SUV lineup. Thankfully, it’s quite good to drive too.

The 2027 Audi Q9 probably should have gone on sale over a decade ago, but better late than never for the extra-long, three-row Audi SUV. Engineered and designed with space-craving Americans in mind, the Q9 clings to a sporty attitude all while nearly filling out the same footprint as a Chevrolet Tahoe. It’s a bit of a balancing act, but made a touch easier by launching with two different versions: Q9 and SQ9. You can read about the latter here, and while its V-8 is always going to be a temptation, the regular Q9 is all the three-row most buyers in this part of the market will need and more.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The Q9 is no slouch in base form, which is only right considering the nearly-$90,000 starting price. There’s no pokey four-cylinder option; instead, it gets Audi’s potent 2.9-liter twin-turbo V-6 as the standard engine. This motor can be found all across the VW Group, but most notably in sportier offerings from Porsche and Audi. Here, it makes 429 hp and 442 lb-ft of torque. Audi channels this power through an eight-speed automatic transmission onward to all four wheels via the Quattro all-wheel-drive system. Audi claims a 0–60 time of only 4.9 seconds, and while that’s 1.1 seconds slower than the V-8-powered SQ9, any three-row SUV that gets to 60 in under five is worthy of celebrating.

Transmission: Eight-speed auto, all-wheel drive

Audis tend to have a universal sense of solidity from behind the wheel, and the Q9 adopts this familiar demeanor. It feels substantial on the road, in large part because it is. Even by the high standards of luxury three-rows, the Q9 has a commendable sense of isolation. Its multilink front and rear, paired with the standard air suspension and adaptive dampers, sop up poor pavement with the best of them, even riding on 22-inch wheels.

Despite not needing to be particularly agile, the Q9 was still ready to boogie when I flipped it into its Dynamic mode. Surprisingly, the Q9 and SQ9 share the same suspension, which results in the Q9 being nearly as fun to throw around as the SQ9. In one way, it’s actually better than its V-8-powered sibling: weight. The Q9 weighs a few hundred pounds less than the SQ9, and much of that difference is lifted off the front end. So on a twisty section of road, the Q9 responded with greater eagerness than I expected in something so large, and it definitely had a pointier front end than the SQ9.

That said, the regular Q9 also has a more laid-back tune to its Quattro system, one that isn’t as rear-biased as the SQ9’s. I had to be pushing hard to discern much of a difference on paved roads, though. Audi’s senior Quattro engineer, Dieter Weidemann, told me he actually prefers the base Q9’s Quattro system on low-grip surfaces. Something for potential buyers who regularly drive on snow to consider.

The V-6 itself is largely inoffensive outside of some input lag. It is quiet and got this beast up and moving with no wheezing or stress. Thank the peak torque hitting at a low 2000 rpm for that effortless acceleration sensation around town. Fuel economy isn’t out yet, and while it will surely be better than the thirsty SQ9, the V-6 is still going to drink premium fuel at copious rates.

Liking big screens is a prerequisite for loving the Q9’s interior. The monolithic structure that houses both the digital instrument cluster and infotainment system is the first thing you notice upon opening the door. It’s impressive from a size and screen quality perspective, but there’s a ton of wasted space with large areas of shiny black trim all around the displays.

Audi did well to resist an all-touch-control steering-wheel design, maintaining the all-important volume scroll wheel and buttons you can physically press to skip songs. The real tactile high point is the new turn signals that click with such authority and solidity thanks to their chunky design and easily learned action.

That turn signal is shared with other Audis, but high-class, flagship-esque moments can be found all throughout this interior. The Q9 is the first Audi to feature a new seat design that incorporates one of the most thorough massage functions in the game and 4D sound that lets you experience the music physically through speakers in the seats. Optional automatic doors (both front and rear) make opening and closing them a button-operated task, or you can nudge them to prompt the motors to activate. Considering the size and weight of the rear doors (that open a full 90 degrees), it’s a feature I suspect most owners will learn to like more over the course of ownership.

The second row can be made into a serious luxury abode by optioning the captain’s chairs instead of bench seating. These are powered bucket seats that hardly give up a lick of comfort compared to those in front, though I was disappointed to see they don’t feature the same massage/sound feature as the front buckets. When motored up and out of the way, they leave an adult human-size path into the third row, and there’s even room for that same adult to sit back there in relative comfort should you compromise the second-row legroom by a couple of inches. No, I wouldn’t choose a Q9 to haul six adults across the country, but it is well suited to shorter, fully-loaded drives. A four-zone climate-control system is standard, but there’s an available five-zone setup with an independently controlled zone for those in the wayback.

It’s this spacious third row and the cargo area behind it that finally bring Audi over the hump with its biggest SUV. The Q7 left space for kids, but no adult would ever want to spend time in the third row of that car. Now, you can get the Q9, fill it up with people, and still have a respectable amount of room behind that third row for necessary cargo. Just don’t expect Suburban levels of utility.

Audi isn’t aiming to be the sportiest in this segment, which is an honor that still belongs to the BMW X7. But the Q9 is coming to the fight with an armory of tech and good old-fashioned easy luxury. This is the type of car Audi should have built years ago. Better late than never.

But the cabin architecture struggles to scream flagship with a screen setup that’s verging on tacky, from the gauge cluster to the oddly integrated passenger screen. Odd packaging decisions like including two wireless phone chargers as opposed to storage areas seem like a miss for the American market. And this Q9 truly was designed and engineered for America, a fact Audi is happy to tout repeatedly.

The price is right where it needs to be compared to the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS. There’s dynamic fun to be found should you want to find it, but the Q9 doesn’t compromise its ability to be a luxury family car for outright performance. That is surely the smart move here, and I suspect it’ll be the answer for far more folks than the compromised Q7.

The turn signals that project light onto the pavement to the left or right of the car at night are an awesome feature. With distracted driving an unfortunate reality, the better you’re able to get other people’s attention, the safer a lane change can be. Also it’s just flat-out cool that we’re able to project legible messages on the ground to communicate with other drivers on the road now.

#4568. BYD now has 1.02 million workers, more than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla combined

BYD now has more than 1.02 million employees, according to chairman Wang Chuanfu. That’s more people than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla employ combined.

And it’s a big jump from the start of the year. BYD reported about 869,600 employees at the end of 2025, which means the Chinese automaker has added roughly 150,000 people in 10 months while its vehicle sales are down.

Roughly 960,000 of BYD’s people work in China and about 60,000 work abroad. Up to 120,000 of them are R&D engineers, according to Wang, who shared the figures on stage Wednesday at the China Society of Automotive Engineers’ (CSAE) 33rd annual conference. Their work covers battery cells, motors, electronic controls, and semiconductors.

Wang credits vertical integration for that scale. In his telling, keeping batteries, chips, and motors in-house is what took BYD from a battery maker founded in 1994 to the world’s top-selling new energy vehicle brand several years running. He called the company’s rise a microcosm of China’s auto industry going from follower to leader.

BYD’s workforce has been all over the place in the last few years.

The company had about 570,100 employees at the end of 2022 and 703,500 at the end of 2023. Then it went on a hiring spree. We reported in September 2024 that BYD had passed 900,000 employees and claimed the largest R&D workforce of any automaker, with over 110,000 engineers. It ended 2024 with 968,900 people.

Then came the first big cut. BYD’s 2025 annual report showed roughly 869,600 employees at year-end, a drop of about 99,000, mostly in frontline production jobs.

Now it’s back over a million. Data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence put BYD at 911,900 employees at the end of June, so the company added more than 100,000 people in about four months.

The gap with legacy automakers is massive. Volkswagen Group, which counts its Chinese joint ventures, reported 662,942 employees at the end of 2025. Toyota had 390,927 as of March 31, 2026, and Stellantis had 258,668 at the end of last year.

In the US, Ford ended 2025 with 169,000 employees and GM with 156,000. Tesla reported a worldwide headcount of 134,785 in its latest 10-K.

Add up Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla and you get about 851,000 people. BYD has roughly 170,000 more than that.

But headcount isn’t output. If you divide 2025 global vehicle sales by year-end workforce, BYD comes out far behind:

BYD sold about 4.6 million vehicles last year with 869,600 employees, or 5.3 vehicles per worker. Tesla delivered 1,636,129 vehicles with 134,785 people, about 12 per worker, and Volkswagen Group was at about 13.5. Toyota, with 11.3 million group sales including Daihatsu and Hino, got roughly 29 vehicles out of each employee.

There’s a catch, and it’s a big one. BYD’s headcount isn’t only a car company’s headcount. It includes BYD Electronic, its majority-owned contract manufacturer that assembles devices for other brands and reported 165,000 employees of its own at the end of 2025. It also covers BYD’s battery business, which supplies other automakers, plus its in-house chips, motors, energy storage, and rail transit operations.

In short, BYD’s vertical integration largely drives its high headcount.

BYD sold 3,131,576 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.9% year-over-year. September was its best month of the year at 463,561 units, but the company has been stuck in a brutal price war at home and is losing ground to rivals like Geely and Leapmotor. Its first-half revenue (344.8 billion yuan) and net profit (12.3 billion yuan) were both down year-over-year.

All of the growth is overseas. BYD’s international sales hit 1,342,960 units through September, up 92.7%, and they now make up about 43% of its total volume. That’s on top of BYD beating Tesla on pure EV deliveries again in Q2.

Yet only 60,000 of its 1.02 million workers are based outside China. That’s about 6%. So BYD is still building nearly everything at home and shipping it out, even as its factories in Thailand, Brazil, and Hungary come online.

The 1.02 million number makes for a great headline, but we wouldn’t read it as a sign of strength on its own.

BYD doesn't just make cars. It makes a lot of battery and other parts that go into other things such as other automaker's EVs.

It is automakers, auto supplier, battery makers, electronic contract manufacturer all merged into one.

Remember GM used to make refrigerators and satellites in addition to cars at one point.

BYD’s whole model is to make almost everything itself: cells, chips, motors, seats, and a lot more. That’s a big reason it can sell a Seagull for around $10,000 in China and still make money. But it’s a labor-heavy model, and it works because Chinese factory labor is relatively cheap and plentiful. Toyota gets more than five times as many cars out of each employee. Tesla gets more than twice as many.

The problem is that BYD’s growth is now outside China, and that’s where this model gets tested. Only 6% of its workforce is abroad, yet 43% of its sales are. Tariffs in Europe, Brazil, Mexico, and elsewhere are pushing BYD to build locally, but a factory in Hungary or Brazil won’t necessarily produce the same.

The number that should worry legacy automakers is the 120,000 engineers. That’s almost as many people as Tesla employs in total, all working on product.

For the past two years, the narrative surrounding electric vehicles has been dominated by massive depreciation and sluggish showroom traffic. However, a significant shift is currently underway in the secondary market. As budget-conscious consumers actively seek out affordable alternatives to internal combustion, the demand for pre-owned electric models is suddenly accelerating at an unprecedented pace across the country.

This secondary market boom presents a stark contrast to the new vehicle sector. While expensive brand-new models continue facing long dealership dwell times, the pre-owned electric segment is currently setting records with buyers. Furthermore, as fluctuating fuel costs continue to heavily influence consumer buying habits, this sudden shift in buyer behavior is helping automakers see their EV sales jump when they focus on affordability and value.

According to a recent study by iSeeCars, used EV prices have surprisingly reversed their long downward trajectory, rising by approximately 9.8% overall. The broad takeaway from the report indicates that consumer demand is finally catching up with the available inventory. Buyers who were previously priced out of the electric transition are now enthusiastically scooping up heavily depreciated lease returns.

We have earlier reported that a massive flood of cheap electric vehicles would heavily disrupt residual values and cost manufacturers billions. However, this rising price trend proves that eager buyers are actively stepping in to absorb that inventory. In fact, deliberately adding more affordable used cars to the secondary market can ultimately benefit car companies in the long run by cultivating early brand loyalty. For those consumers who have been patiently waiting for the market to surge, the window to grab absolute rock-bottom pricing might be slowly closing as values naturally stabilize.

The timing of this price stabilization is incredibly critical for the broader automotive ecosystem. Throughout the year, roughly 300,000 used EVs hit dealership lots as early adopter lease programs expire, with more to come in the next few months. If prices had continued their brutal downward spiral, it would have created a catastrophic financial crisis for automotive finance arms and dealership networks alike.

Despite this almost 10% upward swing in used valuations, savvy consumers can still negotiate incredible bargains if they know where to look. By taking advantage of existing tax credits and heavily subsidized dealership promotions, shoppers can easily find the best EV deals available before the secondary market fully rebounds. This price correction proves that electric vehicles are finally establishing a healthy, sustainable lifecycle in the used car sector.

If you want your kids to think the Honda Passport parked in your driveway is more than a run-of-the-mill three-row mid-size SUV, show them a picture of this new race truck, which not only wears the Passport name, but features a front end that faithfully resembles the crossover’s mug. “Daddy’s/mommy’s car is based on a race car,” you can tell them. That’ll be a lie; the Baja Spec shares nothing more than a name with the mainstream Passport. But it’ll also give you street cred in your kids’ mind, ‘cause your car will be associated with the most badass Passport ever made.

See all results for new 2027 Honda Passport for sale near 63129

The Honda Passport Baja Spec is a new state-of-the-art racing machine that was developed to compete in the top Trophy Truck class of the 2027 SCORE World Desert Championship. If you didn’t know, Honda has a long history with Baja racing dating back to the early ‘60s, and it played a role in the first official running of the Baja 1000. Following 22 overall victories in that legendary race, Honda Racing Corporation (HRC) will make its new trophy truck the first hybrid vehicle to compete in California’s premier off-road endurance racing series.

The Passport Baja Spec is powered by a mid-mounted twin-turbocharged 2.4-liter V-6 that’s based on the engine in Acura’s ARX-06 IMSA race car, and it’s paired with an 800-volt hybrid system. The latter features a lightweight battery pack with a carbon-fiber shell that protects pouch cells similar to the ones used in Formula 1 racing. A front-mounted five-speed gearbox sends over 1300 horsepower to all four wheels through an all-wheel-drive transaxle and dual rear driveshafts.

HRC says the Passport Baja Spec introduces new tech to the series, with its roster of innovations including dual-axle brake-by-wire, adaptive traction control, and power that’s deployed by AI. It’s all hidden under a carbon-fiber body that’s adorned with a Red Bull livery; underneath is a 145-gallon safety cell made from carbon Kevlar and developed by Mason Motorsports. To help manage airflow, HRC added side channels behind the front wheels, and tunnels around the cab help reduce aerodynamic drag.

The trophy truck’s ride is controlled by a custom long-travel suspension that features Fox racing dampers. A set of large Toyo tires highlights all four corners, and there’s a backup pair of rubber shoes sticking out the back of the Baja Spec Passport. And speaking of things in the back, HRC positioned fixed-mass components like coolers, batteries, and fluid tanks there to better distribute weight and lower the center of gravity for improved handling.

#4564. When one door closes: Polestar 2 production ends, and epic EV deals

Forget about the 600+ hp hybrid-powered Polestar 1 supercoupe; the car that established Polestar as a standalone brand was the 2. As the brand pulls out of the US and shifts its focus to the rest of the world, it’s time to look back at the EV that helped define Polestar, along with a look around at some of the best EV deals of all time.

A number of European news sites (including Electrive and TV2 Broom) are reporting that the last new Polestar 2 has rolled off the company’s Luqiao assembly line, with more than 200,000 of the all-electric sedan/hatchbacks built in China since the electric sedan launched in 2020. And, while the company hasn’t confirmed that with any sort of official announcement, the news jives with the company’s previously announced plans to release an updated Polestar 2 in 2027, followed by an all-new Polestar 7 SUV that’s set to follow in early 2028.

With the brand set to pull out of the US after the Trump Administration’s Commerce Department declined to grant it authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule earlier this year, it might at first seem like that US Polestar fans will miss out on that freshened 2, whatever shape it takes – but don’t lose hope, yet.

First shown in 2016, the original Volvo Concept 40.2 was supposed to be a new, entry-level sedan for the now Geely-owned Volvo, which was in the process of separating itself from Ford ownership and the Focus-based C30 coupe and S40/V50 sedan and wagons. And a fine entry-level Volvo it would have been, too, if Tesla’s share price hadn’t made it worth more than the next five most valuable car companies combined.

See, once Tesla (or, more to the point, $TSLA) did that, every carmaker in the world figured the stock market would bless them with billions, too, and started announcing plans to go all electric, right now. Volvo parent company Geely, however, decided they’d fast-track the process, taking the next two Volvo models in their pipeline (the C90 coupe version of the S90 sedan and the C40 sedan previewed by the Concept 40.2) and made them Polestars.

A SPAC merger later, and Polestar was spun off as not only its own brand, but its own, largely Chinese-owned company – which brings us to where we are now.

In the US the Polestar 3 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) SUV starts at something like $67,500 and offers a 111 kWh battery pack good for an EPA-rated range of up to 350 miles. The top-shelf Performance-spec Polestar 3, meanwhile, offers an all-wheel-drive dual-motor setup that Polestar rates at 380 kW (~517 hp) that will launch you across suburbia with a 0–60 mph time in the 4 second range, albeit with slightly less range than the base model … but that $67,500 price is really more of a suggestion these days.

Polestar is offering a $23,000 discount on the 3 and a $25,000, rebate, market adjustment or whatever on the 4. That means that you can get a brand new Polestar 3 or 4 with Chinese EV tech and more than a little bit of Volvo safety baked in for a dramatically reduced price. If you pick the right one at the right dealer, probably for less than $40,000.

One of the best looking cars from the last decade… the 2024+ RWD is such a great value…. I got one myself a year ago for $28k with 5k on the odometer.

As for the 2, I have a bit of a personal connection to that one. My son picked up a 19,000 mile 2024 Polestar 2 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) in Glacier for under $22K, which is an absolutely shocking price for a fast, capable sporty sedan hatchback that isn’t just a worthy successor to the S40 it was meant to replace, but a solid foundation for an EV brand that got wrapped up in politics.

Check out the links below to see what kind of deal you can get on a new Polestar near you, and if you’re interested in a 2, you can probably score a great deal there, too. Let us know what you find in the comments.

The electric vehicle market had strong momentum at the start of this decade, with Ford even expanding the Mustang lineup with an EV spin-off called the Mustang Mach-E. Reports also suggest that Chevrolet once considered expanding the Corvette lineup with two new all-electric models, an SUV and a two-door sports car. But apparently, the automaker may have already shelved those plans.

According to GM Authority, plans for the SUV, internally codenamed V224, and the two-door EV, codenamed V284, have been put on hold. A fastback spin-off was also reportedly in the works, though the publication is less certain about its existence. These vehicles were initially expected to launch between 2025 and 2026, but with this year nearing its end, none have materialized so far.

The report also didn’t offer an explanation for why GM reportedly shelved the potential expansion. But given the slowing demand for EVs, especially in the U.S., these models could face less favorable market conditions. The Corvette SUV may be worth looking at, as this type of vehicle continues to see sustained demand. If the SUV version takes off, it could potentially generate revenue to support the Corvette lineup and further expansion plans. Lamborghini demonstrates this lineup dynamic with the Urus, which continues to be its best-selling model over its traditional supercar offerings. However, an all-electric powertrain could introduce additional uncertainties.

In fact, in the third quarter of this year, GM’s EV sales declined 62% compared to the same period last year. Sure, Q3 2025 saw a huge spike in sales as buyers rushed their EV purchases before the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired, but slowing EV sales have also affected other brands. Ford even ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning, while Ram dropped plans for an all-electric 1500 in favor of a range-extended version.

What’s more interesting is that Corvette sales are up. The American sports car sold 6,585 units in Q3 2026, a 28.5% increase over the 5,123 units sold during the same period last year. This could tell the automaker that the current formula is working, and that now may not be the right time to commit resources to developing new models.

However, these reports have not been confirmed by GM itself. One of the automaker’s latest electrification developments involves preparing its Lansing Delta Township Assembly plant for future hybrid production, which could help it capitalize on growing demand for hybrids in the U.S. The Corvette remains its sole hybrid offering with the Grand Sport X and the more extreme ZR1X, the latter capable of generating 1,250 horsepower.

To be fair, reports of the expansion plan date back to 2022, so jumping on the EV bandwagon may have been worth the risk at the time. Times are changing, and seeing the expansion plan reportedly shelved isn’t much of a surprise. However, Corvette chief engineer Tony Roma recently said that the nameplate will eventually go fully electric, but don’t expect it anytime soon.

#4562. New Trek e-bike is first to get Bosch’s new motor with a major power upgrade

Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.

The updated drive system brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.

The Trek Marlin+ has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.

In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.

And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.

The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.

That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.

Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.

The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.

Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.

The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.

For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.

The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.

The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.

Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.

Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.

Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.

With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.

But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

#4560. Clerical Error Means Herta is Still One Point Shy of Super License Following Mexico FP1

One extra step is added to Colton Herta’s journey to F1, following a miscalculation of superlicense points stemming from an IndyCar.com clerical error.

Colton Herta participated in back-to-back Grand Prix Free Practice 1 sessions in Austin and Mexico City, hoping to secure the final superlicense points to potentially move into Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac in 2027.

Cadillac has only confirmed Sergio Perez’s contract extension, as a driver change seems imminent for Bottas ride.

The problem is that, at the start of Herta’s 2026 F2 campaign, the FIA noted he had 35 points toward his license from his last three years of IndyCar competition; at some point, this number was upped to 36 when he truly had 35. A misprint on the IndyCar website had Herta finishing sixth in the championship instead of seventh in 2025. Herta was projected to finish sixth last year, but Felix Rosenqvist's late-season push brought him to sixth in the points instead.

“There was an anomaly in the website database display, which was caught this week and now reflects the official standings as they were published Aug. 31, 2025,” IndyCar said in a statement.

The championship finishes were shown in error at some point over the spring when the FIA did it’s fact-checking and did not look into it again until this weekend, with the 40-point goal in sight.

The FIA used ‘The Way Back Machine’, an online resource to help figure out how they got the math wrong. It showed that the championship standings were changed incorrectly at one point during the summer, but they were correct at the start of the year.

“Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I haven't talked to anybody about it,” Herta told media in Mexico City. “As far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40.”

Herta has struggled in F2, so his only points this year have come from practice sessions. All F1 teams must put rookies in at least four practice sessions over the course of the season. Cadillac has already used one extra session to help Herta reach the superlicence goal, and his Monza run this September wasn't long enough to count for a point. Cadillac must run Herta in one more free practice before the year’s end. Next weekend in Brazil is an easy option, with a lack of support races.

The differences between automotive markets are interesting; some regions require certain cars in segments that don’t sell well elsewhere. In other cases, brands repurpose and revive nameplates they no longer use to enter a segment they want to compete in.

That’s the case for one of Toyota’s most recognized models that had a long run but was recently killed off. The Avalon used to be a staple in Toyota’s lineup, but made way for the Crown’s entry in the U.S.; however, in China, the Avalon lives on and is getting a new model too.

Autohome reports it learned from official brand sources that the new Toyota Avalon for China will launch on November 5. The new Avalon will feature exterior and interior upgrades and offer both gasoline and hybrid variants.

On the outside, the first major change is the redesigned front grille, now featuring vertical chrome slats as the main design element. Above that grille is the now-iconic Toyota C-shaped headlight cluster we see on the Crown and the Camry, to which the Avalon is closely related. Size-wise, the new Avalon measures 4,990 mm (length), 1,850 mm (width), and 1,440 mm (height), with a wheelbase of 2,870 mm. The rims now feature a new design, while the rear lighting cluster sets the Avalon apart from its Toyota sedan siblings with its own distinct pattern and layout.

The Avalon was always supposed to be an elevated Camry, bridging the gap between that model and the higher Lexus cars. That’s evident in the new Avalon’s interior, which features a wraparound design with a large infotainment screen, a HUD, and crystal trim that contrasts with the subtle two-tone piping on the seats and steering wheel. It also has other notable features like heated and ventilated seats, massaging functions for the front passengers, and an in-car fragrance system.

In terms of the powertrain, the Avalon will be offered with either a 2.0-liter gasoline engine that makes 170 hp, which is the same as the current Avalon, or a 2.5-liter gasoline-hybrid system that makes a combined 230 hp. The 2.0-liter gets a normal CVT, while the hybrid gets a specialized e-CVT.

#4558. BYD (BYDDY) Q3 profit jumps 28% on exports, but inventory balloons 60%

BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.

But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.

BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.

BYD filed its third-quarter report with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Thursday. Here are the key figures for July through September:

That’s BYD’s best quarterly profit since the end of 2024, and the first time revenue has grown year-over-year after four straight quarters of declines.

It’s also a big rebound from the start of the year. BYD’s Q1 2026 profit collapsed 55% to ¥4.08 billion, before recovering to ¥8.24 billion in Q2.

Still, it came in under expectations. Brokerages polled by Reuters were looking for ¥11.4 billion to ¥12.95 billion.

And zoom out to the full year so far, and BYD is treading water. Revenue for the first nine months was ¥566.30 billion, up just 0.01%, while net profit fell 4.2% to ¥22.34 billion. That’s on top of 2025, when BYD’s annual profit had already dropped to ¥32.62 billion from ¥40.25 billion in 2024.

The quarterly report doesn’t break out vehicle volumes, but BYD’s monthly sales filings do. The automaker sold 1,323,065 vehicles in Q3, up 18.7% from 1,114,192 a year earlier.

All of that growth, and then some, came from outside China. BYD exported 550,704 vehicles in the quarter, up 137% from 232,806 in Q3 2025. Everything else, which is mostly the Chinese market, fell about 12% to roughly 772,000 units.

Exports now account for 42% of BYD’s sales. In the first half, overseas markets already brought in ¥181.3 billion, or 53% of the company’s revenue.

For perspective, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in Q3. BYD exported more cars than Tesla sold on the entire planet.

At home, it’s a different story. China’s price war hasn’t let up, and BYD is now fighting it with cars like the new Seagull with 5-minute flash charging, starting under $10,000. That’s great for buyers. Not so much for margins.

BYD doesn’t report gross margin in its quarterly filing, but it can be calculated from the income statement. We get about 18.0% for Q3, slightly better than 17.6% a year ago, but down from roughly 18.9% in Q2.

The bigger hits are further down the income statement.

Finance expenses came in at ¥7.37 billion for the first nine months, compared to a ¥2.94 billion gain in the same period last year. BYD blames exchange losses. That’s a swing of more than ¥10 billion when the company made ¥22.34 billion in profit, which is the price of doing half your business in foreign currencies.

Impairment charges are also climbing. BYD booked ¥2.71 billion in asset impairment losses, up 68%, which it says is mostly inventory write-downs because of “the expanded inventory scale.” Credit losses tripled to ¥944 million, set aside “in line with the increase in trade receivables.”

And then there’s R&D. BYD’s research and development expenses fell 17% to ¥36.28 billion over nine months. A small part of that is accounting, since BYD capitalized more development costs on its balance sheet this year, but it’s still a notable drop for a company that has built its brand on vertical integration and in-house tech.

Here’s how a few key line items moved between Dec. 31, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026:

BYD attributes both the inventory and receivables jumps “mainly” to the growth of its overseas auto business. That makes sense. Cars on ships, in ports and at foreign dealers sit on the books a lot longer than a car sold to a dealer in China.

The bills payable number stands out too. Those are short-term notes BYD hands suppliers instead of cash, and they more than tripled this year, which BYD explains as “the increase in settlement of bills.”

On the financing side, BYD cut its short-term bank borrowings roughly in half to ¥18.67 billion, but tripled its bonds outstanding to ¥14.99 billion and issued super short-term commercial paper.

To be fair, there are healthy signals in there as well. Operating cash flow for the first nine months was ¥54.47 billion, up 33%. Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) rose 81% to ¥92.95 billion, which points to strong orders. And cash spent on new factories and equipment fell 24% to ¥87.38 billion as BYD’s huge buildout slows down.

On the surface, this is a good quarter for BYD. Profit is up 28%, revenue is growing again, and the export strategy is clearly working. BYD exporting more cars in a quarter than Tesla sells worldwide would have sounded absurd just three years ago.

But we don’t think it’s as clean as the headline number suggests.

BYD had a rocket like ascension and sales exploded while they kept on introducing better technology. Considering the competition increase, they are still doing very well. They are not even everywhere yet but that is probably coming at some point soon too.

BYD added over ¥83 billion worth of inventory in nine months while its sales were down 3.9% year-to-date. Receivables are up, supplier IOUs are up, and cash is way down. That’s what it looks like when you push a lot of cars into a long overseas pipeline and wait to get paid for them. It works as long as those cars sell at decent prices. If they don’t, those impairment charges we’re already seeing get a lot bigger.

And the domestic business isn’t getting easier. BYD is selling fewer cars in China than a year ago while it now employs over 1 million people. The cuts to R&D spending are a sign the company is looking for savings somewhere.

These are all signs of BYD’s business changing. It is going to take a while for it to settle, but I think they are currently in a great spot with the switch to their Blade battery 2.0 virtually over, and new capacity coming from Hungary, Thailand, and Brazil.

Audi has managed to bend light by putting its curved OLED panels on the Q9, making it the first production vehicle to have such a feature.

Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol Ditches Roof and Luxury for Serious Off-Roading

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

When it comes to lighting innovations, Audi has many accomplishments, especially with LEDs. For instance, the D3 (second-gen) Audi A8 was the very first car to feature LED daytime running lights. After that, it was the first-generation R8 that became that had full LED illumination, front and rear.

Then, the third-generation A8 became the first production car with matrix LED lighting, after that, the TT RS became one of the first cars to have OLED tail lights. In other words, Audi has done a lot for the world of vehicle lighting, and many of its innovations have become commonplace today.

It seems that the folks from Ingolstadt want to keep its lighting innovations streak going by introducing yet another world-first. Its latest bit of lighting tech can be seen in the Q9, and it’s the very first one in the world to be available with curved OLED exterior lighting. While that doesn’t sound all too exciting, this has all the potential to change how rear lights are lit and designed.

One could say that this has allowed Audi to bend light, figuratively speaking, of course. By curving the OLED panel, it lets brake lights and turn signals be more visible from the corners of the vehicle. But the main advantage of doing this is surface uniformity, and OLEDs deliver uniform illumination without the need for point bulbs or reflectors.

The carrier glass of these OLEDs measures just 0.1 millimeters thick, which is 1/256ths of an inch. For easier visualization, that’s roughly the thickness of a hair strand, and that’s allowed Audi to ‘bend’ the panel to a significant degree. That allows the panel to follow the contours of the vehicle, as well as giving designers more freedom to explore more daring light designs.

As Audi has been making OLEDs for a decade now, it’s learned enough to move the technology forwards. Now in it’s the third-iteration, the Q9 boasts the has the largest OLED panel Audi has built to date. It has a total of 512 segments spread across six digital OLED panels. The individually controllable segments give the Q9’s rear lights multiple static, active, or semi-active digital light signatures, as well as project warning symbols.

It’s worth pointing out that these curved OLEDs are not fitted to all Q9 trims. If you want these lights, you can only get these in the Prestige model, as it’s not optional on both base Premium and mid-spec Premium Plus variants. These lights are fitted as standard in the SQ9.
