#4556. Toyota’s 5 Woodland SEMA Concepts Are Giving Almost-Rugged Vibes

The Crown Signia, bZ Woodland, Grand Highlander, RAV4, and Sienna get prepped for the great outdoors with mild but effective mods.

The whole “getting outside” thing has seen an enormous resurgence in popularity in recent years, so Toyota figured it couldn’t go wrong by modifying a handful of its mainstream models to reflect the crunchy vibe.

Naturally, the project was entrusted to the staff of its CALTY Design Research arm, who explored the idea of how daily drivers—primarily the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, bZ Woodland, and Crown Signia—could be modified to better perform in and near the boonies without compromising their on-road comfort and usability.

See all results for new 2026 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid for sale near 94112

Despite their obvious differences, the team started with a single-shot approach covering each model in a coat of Horizon Blue paint, inspired by a hue used in the 1960s on Toyota models like the Stout, Crown, and Corona. A contrasting black is used for the roofs and hoods. The shared modifications include lift kits, large overfenders, stylized satin-black wheels, all-terrain tires, roof racks, and cross bars. Each also wears a “Woodland” logo badge on its tailgate.

Toyota didn’t offer details or specifics regarding the modifications, but even causal viewers will recognize the Yakima logo on the roof racks and the Yokohama Geolander X-AT tires mounted to the Toyota-branded wheels, complete with tiny “Woodland” badges on the rims of some models. Look closely, or you’ll miss low-profile driving lights deftly worked into the Crown Signia’s fasciae just above the grille.

As SEMA exercises go, the Woodland treatment is pretty mild, but likely is intended to gauge public perception of some simple modifications that could possibly be earmarked for future production and sale through official Toyota dealers and channels. If that theory proves correct, sign us up for the sweet Sienna Woodland in all its minivan glory.

#4554. The Ford Escape may return as an EV based on the UEV platform [Update]

Ford pulled the plug on the Escape last year after a 25-year run, but the crossover SUV could return as an EV on the new UEV platform.

While Ford is preparing to launch the Fathom, its first vehicle based on the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform in 2027, the company is already hinting at what could be its second UEV-based model.

The last gas-powered Escape models rolled off the production line at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant as it retooled the facility to prepare for the new Fathom electric pickup.

Typically, when Ford retires a model, its landing page says something like “we’re discontinuing” it, or “it’s the end of the road,” such as with the Edge SUV.

Meanwhile, the Escape landing page says the “SUV may be taking a breather for now,” declaring the “Ford Escape is tapping the brakes,” with no mention of it being discontinued. Instead, the site directs you to check out Ford’s other vehicles while it’s on hiatus.

According to Ford Authority, the Escape will return as an all-electric crossover SUV based on the UEV platform.

Update 10/29/2026: A Ford spokesperson told Electrek that the Ford Authority report is pure speculation and the company has not announced the Escape will return as an EV or that it will be based on the UEV platform.

If it does come to life, the Ford Escape EV would likely remain close in size to the outgoing gas model, which measures 180.1″ long, 74.1″ wide (without mirrors), and 66.1″ tall, with a 106.7″ wheelbase. That’s about the size of other compact SUVs like the Toyota RAV4 and Hyundai Tucson.

The report claimed the electric Escape is expected to enter production at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in 2029, possibly making it the second vehicle based on its UEV platform, following the Fathom pickup.

CEO Jim Farley confirmed on Ford’s Q3 earnings call on Wednesday that the Fathom launch “remains on track for the fourth quarter of next year.”

The Fathom is “a breakthrough product,” Farley said, adding the pickup is highly capable, innovative, and affordable.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range version. With the $1,595 delivery fee, Ford’s electric pickup will still start under $30,000, which the company says will be “right in the heart of the market.”

The Fathom will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps into its navigation system. It will also be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving. Other standard features include Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Ford claims the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, not including the added bed and frunk (front trunk).

2029 seems a little slow, but I'm glad Ford is still pushing ahead with EV plans.

Inside, the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with an easy-to-use navigation system using Apple Maps.

Ford has yet to reveal battery specs or range, but the UEV platform uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to reduce costs. We also know the Fathom will have an NACS charge port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

The UEV platform is flexible enough to underpin vehicles ranging from compact crossovers to pickup trucks and vans, so an electric Escape would make sense.

With the Fathom set to launch next year, we should learn more about the potential Ford Escape EV soon. Check back for updates.

American car production has always been an important part of competing in the local automotive market. Any car maker that wants to be taken seriously and sell in decent numbers needs a manufacturing plant, which is why most major brands have multiple facilities scattered across the U.S.

The Trump administration has been pushing its agenda to ensure that American jobs are safe and increase. As part of the government’s plan, it aims to ensure America keeps building cars, and we’re seeing carmakers respond with new or refreshed plants to protect the manufacturing future.

Hyundai’s U.S. base is in Montgomery, Alabama, with a 2 million square foot footprint and the capacity to produce 400,000 cars and 700,000 engines annually. Yet the South Korean manufacturer just announced it wants to expand the Alabama plant with a sizable $500 million investment. The new investment will “support future vehicle production, expand engine manufacturing capabilities, and advance next-generation propulsion technologies at the Montgomery manufacturing facility.”

The fresh capital injection will bring Hyundai’s total investment in Alabama to a respectable $2.2 billion since it began operations in 2005. Hyundai isn’t done yet, with plans to bring its investment in the U.S. to $2.6 billion between 2025 and 2028, as Hyundai Motor Company President and CEO José Muñoz announced. Mark Rader, president and CEO of Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Alabama, said the new investment will ensure HMMA remains a cornerstone of Hyundai’s North American manufacturing operations for years to come.

In essence, the new investment will retool the Alabama plant to support production of Extended Range Electric Vehicle (EREV) technology and the new Tucson and refreshed Santa Fe models. These two cars are important for the Hyundai brand in the U.S., with the Tucson remaining their best-selling model and the Santa Fe close behind. According to the Hyundai U.S. group, the all-new Tucson is set to begin production before the year closes out.

Hyundai’s EREV technology is set to usher in a new era for the brand. The EREV tech that Hyundai will develop and build promises to be different from the current crop of range-extending powertrains. Hyundai’s EREV aims to be more compact, lighter, and more energy-efficient.

#4550. Driven: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid Is the Best Nissan on Sale Today

Nissan’s e-Power hybrid powertrain transforms the Rogue into a legitimate contender for the segment’s throne.

There’s confidence, and then there’s whatever Nissan is doing. The automaker is so confident in the 2027 Rogue Hybrid that it included a fleet of hybrid Toyota RAV4s for comparison. To say this is a rare event is underselling it. But, as it turns out, Toyota (and Honda) should be on high alert. This fourth-generation Rogue is quiet, comfortable, and most of all, refined in a way that punches well above the rest of the Nissan lineup.

The new Rogue Hybrid couldn’t come at a better time for Nissan. While Toyota and Honda have both been able to sell hybrid crossovers in the hundreds of thousands each year, Nissan took a different route, most recently settling for a rebadged Mitsubishi Outlander plug-in hybrid model. However, the Rogue Hybrid has a trick up its sleeve for 2027, one that we think has real legs.

The secret behind the new Rogue’s competence is its e-Power series-hybrid powertrain. This third generation of Nissan’s multi-energy system is the first on offer in the States. The powertrain starts with a turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder engine running on the Miller cycle, which serves as a generator to feed power to a compact lithium-ion battery pack. In turn, that battery sends power to a pair of electric drive motors—one on the front axle and one on the rear—giving the Rogue a full-time all-wheel-drive setup with independent motor control.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid for sale near 76210

This isn’t the same gas engine as in the brand’s other models. Nissan’s engineers told us that while the automaker does have another turbocharged 1.5-liter three-banger on the shelf, the two powerplants have little in common. For starters, the Rogue’s engine sports a larger turbocharger; one downside of bigger snails is that they take more time to spool before providing boost (and thus torque), but because the Rogue’s engine never powers the wheels, continually needing to build boost is not an issue. Nissan was able to tune the engine to spend most of its time between 2000 and 5000 rpm, which also keeps the engine’s harmonics in check and mitigates noise, vibration, and harshness.

In practice, the e-Power system is great. There are five levels of regeneration, including a true one-pedal driving mode. Thanks to the electric traction motors, Nissan developed what it calls Smooth Stop. The tech manages the final moments of deceleration to control the vehicle’s pitch and reduce any head bob when coming to a halt.

Press the right pedal, and with a combined 225 horsepower, accelerating from a stop is smooth yet perky. Nissan quotes a 60-mph time of 6.4 seconds—which would make it quicker than both the RAV4 and CR-V Hybrid—but we’ll have to wait until we can subject one to our testing regimen before we verify that figure. Even without our equipment, we can tell that the Rogue has plenty of getup. That instant e-motor torque means highway passing is a breeze. Plus, the system is zippy without giving up much in terms of fuel efficiency: The midrange SR trim earns an EPA-estimated 41 mpg city, 36 highway, and 38 combined; the SV and Platinum trims are down 1 mpg on the highway and in their combined ratings, making the Rogue not quite a class leader but not too far off either.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid for sale near 76210

On the curvy roads surrounding Santa Barbara, California, the Rogue handled itself well. The steering is a bit lifeless, but it’s no worse than the rest of the segment. Hustle the Rogue through a particularly tight curve, and the rear-axle torque vectoring will keep understeer to a minimum. We’re hesitant to speak too favorably of the Rogue’s ride quality, given the dearth of broken pavement we traversed, but we came away with no real grievances against the crossover’s suspension and high hopes for its composure over the poorly maintained roads around our home office.

The Rogue’s new interior is less impressive than its powertrain and driving demeanor, but we’ve got little to complain about. Nissan did a good job of hiding any cost-cutting here. Faux leather on the seats might be an expectation, but in here, the material extends to the door trim, center console, dashboard, and even the side of the central tunnel. Also, card-carrying members of the Piano Black Haters Club will appreciate a total lack of fingerprint magnets. The cabin is also a practical space, with up to 66 cubic feet of storage when the second row is folded down. Parents will appreciate that the rear doors open nearly 90 degrees, giving plenty of room to install or remove a car seat.

The base SV and mid-level SR trims come with a 12.3-inch touchscreen setup, though the SR model we drove was optioned with a 14.3-inch unit (standard on the Platinum) running a Google-based OS with support for wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The resolution is crisp, and the screen is plenty responsive, but our favorite part of the cockpit is situated below the displays. There, Nissan equipped the new Rogue with dedicated physical controls for the heated and cooled seats, temperature, fan speed, and climate-control modes. The wireless phone charger located at the front of the center console includes magnets, and they work wonders to prevent your phone from sliding around like a greased pig (the Platinum trim gets dual wireless phone chargers). While we will never hate on the presence of switchgear, we do wish the array felt a bit nicer to manipulate.

We found the Rogue’s seats plenty comfortable, even after a full day of driving. Wind and tire noise are hushed, allowing for quiet conversations while keeping driving fatigue to a minimum. Still, for as mitigated as they are, wind and tire noise are more prevalent in the cabin than engine noise, which is seemingly kept under lock and key about two towns over. There’s so little engine NVH that most passengers shouldn’t notice when the turbo three-pot kicks on to power the battery.

The Rogue Hybrid is priced attractively too. Since Nissan wants the next-generation nonhybrid Rogue to serve as the model’s entry point, there’s no generic S trim for the hybrid. Instead, the electrified Rogue lineup starts at $37,065 with the SV variant. The SR (the trim we drove) will be the first trim to arrive and will start at $39,065. The SV and the $45,065 Platinum won’t arrive until January.

There’s no doubt about it: The 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid isn’t just the most compelling product in Nissan’s lineup; it’s compelling, period. You’ll notice we didn’t even bother talking about the Toyota that sat right next to it.

#4549. Leclerc Given FIA Minimum Penalty for Leaving the Track and Taking the Lead at the Mexico City GP

Neither his teammate nor Max Verstappen is happy that the FIA chose not to give Charles Leclerc a 10-second penalty for his opening-lap move.

At the start of the Mexico City Grand Prix, Charles Leclerc moved up from third to challenge his teammate Lewis Hamilton for the lead. And as has often been the case between the two Ferrari drivers this year, the battle could’ve gone cleaner.

Charles Leclerc took the lead by leaving the track in turn four, pushing Hamilton off his line and sending the pole-sitter tumbling back to third, with Max Verstappen taking advantage.

Quickly, Leclerc pulled out to a one-second lead over Verstappen. Leclerc had until turn 12 to give back the position, but with Verstappen down, he would drop from the lead to third.

Leclerc stayed in the lead, and the Stewards investigated his pass; recently, the FIA has had a stern talk with drivers and said that nearly every advantage gained by leaving the track that the driver did not reverse in time would result in a ten-second penalty.

Leclerc received a 5-second penalty, which was relayed over the radio to the drivers once he was 3.6 seconds clear of Verstappen and 5.1 seconds clear of his teammate Hamilton.

The mitigating circumstances for the league minimum of 5 seconds seem to be the nature of the opening turns at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

“Ha, I thought all the new penalties were a ten?” Verstappen replied over the radio to the news.

Neither Hamilton nor Leclerc ended up winning the race, with Hamilton finishing second and Leclerc fourth.

With his podium finish, Hamilton was asked about missing out on the win because of his teammate’s move and unwillingness to give back the position which ultimately led to a Ferrari loss.

“I mean, in the drivers' briefing we discussed that as soon as you go off in turn one, you have to give the position back, but obviously.” Hamilton referred to Leclerc’s 5-second penalty, “Last year I got a 10-second penalty for that same move that he did. But ultimately, it was that that cost us the win today. And I think we have to have some serious talks behind the scenes for sure.”

Post-race in the press conference, Hamilton expanded on his issue with Leclerc’s first-lap move and his subsequent move on the red-flag restart, saying that it has more to do with mentality than age.

“The guy’s 28 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. I think it’s a mentality thing. It’s like do-or-die: either I win, or none of us do, and it shouldn’t be that. It should be us getting that one-two.”

With Hamilton in second place in the WDC challenge ahead of a Mercedes, his bitterness towards teamwork has grown over the season.

Subaru wants to plug the holes in its lineup and win over drivers of all ages, coast to coast. It’s a bold move for a brand that’s usually stuck to its niche. The automaker’s challenge now is to cast a wider net without losing the quirky charm that made it a household name in the first place.

Subaru’s also sharpening its pencil with the Cost Innovation 20-30 plan, aiming to slash about ¥200 billion ($1.26 billion) a year from its expenses by 2030. That extra cash could help cushion the blow from rising costs and those pesky US tariffs.

Subaru’s already got a strong identity in America, but snagging 5% of the market means luring in folks who’ve never given the brand a second thought. At this point, Subaru’s been making changes to its pricing, with base models being reintroduced for the 2027 model, lowering the price of entry.

Subaru has to walk a fine line: attract new fans without alienating the loyalists. Just tossing more models into the mix won’t cut it if they don’t bring something special to the table. Its production changes and cost-cutting efforts are sensible steps, particularly as automakers face pressure from tariffs and shifting demand. However, the bigger challenge will be making the lineup relevant to a wider audience.

Subaru knows what it wants and has a roadmap to get there. Whether it can actually poach buyers from the big names will come down to the cars it rolls out and how well they click with American drivers.

McMurtry Automotive is officially celebrating its tenth anniversary, and the high-performance world is far better for it. What began in 2016 as a tiny team of ambitious engineers in rural Gloucestershire, England, has transformed into the manufacturer of arguably the most violent and capable track car ever conceived. Over the last decade, the boutique brand expanded to nearly 100 employees and recently opened a state-of-the-art production facility in the Cotswolds, proving that a small, independent automaker can still disrupt the global hypercar establishment.

The company’s original goal was simple but seemingly impossible: build the ultimate lightweight driver’s vehicle. When their initial superbike-on-four-wheels concept didn’t commercially pan out, the late engineering pioneer and co-founder Sir David McMurtry offered a delightfully blunt solution to solve their traction limitations: “just suck it to the ground.” Inspired by banned 1970s racing technology, the team pivoted to fan-based downforce, creating a platform that would fundamentally change the performance landscape.

By engineering a proprietary “Downforce on Demand” system, McMurtry created a vehicle that literally vacuums itself to the tarmac. Twin electric fans pull air from underneath the chassis, generating a staggering 4,400 pounds of downforce while the vehicle sits at a complete standstill. This allows the almost production-ready electric drivetrain to deploy its 1,000 horsepower instantly, launching the ultra-lightweight carbon fiber chassis from zero to 60 mph in a brain-scrambling 1.55 seconds.

While Tesla promises their upcoming Roadster will use cold-gas thrusters to literally blow the competition away, McMurtry took the exact opposite approach; they built a hypercar that simply sucks. The on-track results of this extreme vacuum engineering have been nothing short of historic. The Spéirling shattered the outright hillclimb record at the Goodwood Festival of Speed in 2022, then smashed the long-standing Top Gear Test Track record. It generates so much instantaneous cornering grip that it even leaves veteran racing drivers speechless, with extreme sports legend Travis Pastrana claiming it is the fastest they’ve driven.

After a decade of relentless prototyping and high-speed testing, the pure fan car is finally transitioning from a wild concept into a tangible reality for well-heeled enthusiasts. Production of the Spéirling PURE is officially underway at the brand’s new UK facility, with the very first customer deliveries slated to begin later this year. Production is strictly capped at just 100 units worldwide, ensuring the vehicle remains an incredibly rare sight at local track days.

From an editorial perspective, McMurtry’s ten-year journey is a massive victory for independent automotive engineering. In an era where legacy manufacturers are constantly adding weight and complexity to their vehicles, McMurtry took a massive financial risk to build a pure, single-seat track weapon. Access to this unparalleled, Formula 1-level performance obviously comes at an astronomical cost, carrying a massive $1.3 million sticker before personalization. However, for the lucky few who can afford it, they are buying a literal piece of physics-defying history.

The year started with Mercedes dominance as teams struggled to catch up in the development race under the new 2026 regulations. Through 19th rounds, Kimi Antonelli won nine races and finished on the podium in 16 races to secure the championship with four races remaining on the calendar.

He did all of this in his second season in F1, just five years after graduating from karts to car racing.

#4541. Ex-Tesla Autopilot head calls vision-only a ‘weird religious stance’

GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, who ran Tesla’s Autopilot program in 2015 and 2016, says dropping radar for a camera-only self-driving system is “a weird religious stance that ignores physics.”

It’s the bluntest rebuke of Tesla’s vision-only bet yet from someone who helped build the original Autopilot. And it lands while Tesla is pushing camera-only Cybercabs into driverless service in Austin.

Anderson made the comments in an interview with The Verge published October 27, after GM’s technology event in New York the week before. Asked whether GM could eventually move to a vision-only approach like Tesla’s, he didn’t leave much room for interpretation.

“If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations,” Anderson said. He added that radar is so cheap that removing it makes no sense, and that “cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can.”

He also said lidar helps camera systems improve faster when the two are trained together. That’s a direct counter to Tesla’s argument that cameras plus fleet data are all you need.

Anderson isn’t a lidar startup CEO talking his book. He led the Model X program at Tesla, then directed Autopilot during its formative years before co-founding self-driving company Aurora. GM hired him as chief product officer in 2025, and Bloomberg reported last year that Mary Barra sees him as a frontrunner to become GM’s next CEO.

His roadmap at GM goes the other way from Tesla’s. The Cadillac Escalade IQ is due to debut GM’s “eyes-off” system in 2028, with lidar, radar, and cameras.

He took a shot at another Tesla habit in the same interview. Anderson said he avoids “eyes off” marketing language altogether, arguing that a driver-assist system that feels very capable already pushes drivers into complacency. That’s the core problem with selling “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

Tesla started pulling radar from Model 3 and Model Y in May 2021. Tesla Vision launched with limitations: Autosteer capped at 75 mph, a longer minimum following distance, and Smart Summon and Emergency Lane Departure Avoidance disabled at delivery. Ultrasonic sensors went next, in 2022.

The decision wasn’t unanimous inside Tesla. Former employees said engineers tried to convince Elon Musk not to drop radar, and he overruled them. Musk told Electrek at the time that “a very high resolution radar would be better than pure vision, but such a radar does not exist.” We argued that there are plenty of high resolution radars these days.

But the bigger problem is the exact one Anderson named: visibility.

In March, NHTSA upgraded its investigation into FSD in reduced-visibility conditions to an Engineering Analysis covering 3,203,754 vehicles, the last step before a recall. The probe now counts nine crashes, including a pedestrian killed in November 2023. NHTSA found FSD’s camera degradation detection “did not detect common roadway conditions that impaired camera visibility,” including sun glare, fog, and airborne dust, and only alerted drivers right before the crashes.

Radar doesn’t care about sun glare. That’s the point of redundancy.

As a human with 40+ years of driving with vision only, on dark rural roads in bad weather, there have been plenty of times when I had a few moments of confusion / optical illusion. The main thing I've learned is not to panic or make sudden inputs, maybe just let off the gas. The road probably does what it logically should do. Within a few seconds, the real situation usually becomes clear.

My point in saying this is that vision only isn't great, even for humans. I'm not sure a machine can be trained to handle these moments well, and requiring an unprepared "driver" to step in at the last second cannot be expected to end well.

Anderson is right, and he’s in a better position than almost anyone to say it. He ran Autopilot back when it still used radar.

The vision-only case always rested on a tidy idea: humans drive with two eyes, so cameras and enough AI should do the job. But humans crash in fog and glare too, and the promise was always to be far safer than humans, not just as good. Removing a cheap sensor that directly measures velocity, overruling your own engineers to do it, and ending up with a 3.2-million-vehicle NHTSA investigation into cameras that can’t tell when they’re blind isn’t first-principles engineering. It’s a position Musk staked out in 2019 when he called lidar a “fool’s errand,” and he’s been defending it ever since.

Tesla’s own behavior has drifted anyway. It’s building its own fleet maps after years of mocking them, and its Robotaxi runs inside geofences like everyone else’s. Meanwhile, Waymo, with lidar, radar, and cameras, has logged roughly 271 million rider-only miles. Tesla has about 3 million driverless miles since it started pulling safety monitors in January.

Although it didn’t explicitly confirm the name of the upcoming model, codenamed HE1i, it’s expected to go on sale as the IONIQ P as the latest addition to Hyundai’s dedicated IONIQ EV lineup.

Mr. Tarun Garg, Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer of Hyundai Motor India, declared on Wednesday that the “Launch of Bayon marks the onset of our golden product cycle. He added We are also fully geared up for the launch of [our] dedicated mass market EV in Q4 FY27.”

The vehicle was first spotted earlier this year driving near Hyundai’s Sriperumbudur plant in Chennai, India, the “Detroit of Asia,” as it’s known.

Hyundai has yet to confirm the name, but the vehicle carried an “HE1i” tag, suggesting it was an IONIQ model.

Previous electric test vehicles, like the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, were tagged with “ME” and “NE,” with the “E” indicating they are based on the dedicated E-GMP platform.

The new entry-level EV will sit below the Creta Electric as a smaller, lower-priced electric SUV that will serve as a cornerstone of Hyundai’s growth plans in India.

During its CEO Investor Day in August, Hyundai Motor announced plans to launch 100 new or refreshed vehicles between now and 2030, including 58 in North America, 49 in South Korea, 41 in Europe, and 26 in India.

Alongside the recently launched IONIQ 3 and new Tucson, Hyundai previewed a new electric A-SUV for India, a global B-SUV, and another B-SUV for Europe.

Hyundai Motor is investing $15.5 billion to expand its presence in India by 2032, including expanding manufacturing capacity and building a local supply chain. The new entry-level EV will be Hyundai’s first produced locally in India. By 2030, Hyundai expects total production capacity to reach 1.1 million units in India.

Hyundai’s global sales fell 10% year over year in the third quarter to 931,211 units. India, meanwhile, was its fastest-growing market with sales up 9.5% in Q3 to over 150,000 units.

Will Hyundai bring the compact electric SUV to other global markets? The company said India will serve as an “important export hub,” but didn’t offer any further details.

A covered prototype was recently caught testing in South Korea by ShortsCar, initially thought to be the IONIQ 4 or possibly IONIQ 1.

Hyundai already exports vehicles made in India to global markets like the UK, Central and South America, and the Middle East, so it wouldn’t be a surprise.

In September, Hyundai’s domestic sales and exports from India rose 11% to 77,916, the highest monthly total yet.

The Cybercab might be a robotaxi, but some of its hardware is coming to cars you can actually buy. In a bid to simplify building and powering its cars, Tesla is looking to incorporate certain components designed for its Cybercab in its passenger vehicles.

According to Drive Tesla Canada, Nick Verzini, Tesla’s head of drive unit engineering, said on a Munro Live factory tour that a new printed circuit board assembly and power stage will enter Model 3 production in 2026. They come from the inverter Tesla designed for the Cybercab it has started building.

The inverter turns the battery’s DC power into AC that spins the motor, so it affects efficiency and cost. Verzini said the new design has substantially fewer electronic components than the current Model 3 inverter, though no figure was given, and it accepts parts from multiple suppliers. When asked whether the whole unit could fit a Model Y drive unit, he said: “We kept the entire interface.” Tesla hasn’t announced a Model Y change as yet.

Don’t expect a range jump. According to reports, efficiency, range, and price figures remain the same. What fewer parts and multiple suppliers could mean, though Tesla hasn’t promised it, is simpler and cheaper-to-build cars, with less exposure to supply chain volatility. For the Cybercab, Tesla’s 2025 Impact Report reportedly targets at least 6.1 miles per kWh, an efficiency figure that is crucial for a car meant to run all day.

Not everything carries over. The Cybercab’s front-mounted motor uses an 11:1 gear ratio, versus about 9:1 in many other Teslas, and swaps the electric oil pump for a mechanical one. Motor cooling channels also move into a cheaper aluminium housing. Those changes aren’t confirmed for other models. The real test is whether or not these changes will result in real-world gains in reliability, pricing, and/or efficiency.

#4536. Used EVs Are Selling Faster Than Gas Cars or Hybrids

A recent study claims that used EVs are moving off the market much faster than gas or hybrid cars, despite higher prices.

Shoppers in the market for a used car are reportedly shifting toward electric powertrains. A report from iSeeCars claims that EVs are the quickest-moving cars in the used-car market compared with their gas and hybrid counterparts, despite a higher price point than last year.

The report studied over 1.5 million cars between one and five years old to find trends in the current used-car market. Between September 2025 and September 2026, used EVs saw a 9.8 percent price increase, while hybrid prices rose 4.9 percent and gas-powered prices rose less than half a percent. EVs sold for an average of $32,533 in September 2026, landing right in the middle of the more expensive hybrids at $34,476 and less expensive gas-powered vehicles at $31,954.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Though EV prices are increasing, they’re moving off sales floors a lot faster than gasoline models that have stayed relatively the same price. In September 2026, used EVs averaged 41.9 days on the market, which is 13 days less than gas-powered cars. Hybrids find themselves in the middle with about 48.6 days on the market. Compared with September 2025, used EVs sold 10.1 percent faster, while gas cars saw a 19.9 percent longer sales window.

However, gas-powered cars take up the top two spots on the overall fastest-selling cars list. The Lexus IS500, which saw its last production year in 2025, took the top spot, followed by the Audi A4 Allroad, another gasoline model. The Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback sits in third place as the first EV on the list, spending an average of 29.8 days on the market. Gas-powered cars may have dominated the top two spots, but EVs still managed to sell faster overall than the gas-powered herd.

The fastest-selling EVs recorded were the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron, followed by the Toyota bZ4X, and the Lexus RZ 300e. The Model 3’s price increased by about $3870.

EV prices started rising in April 2026 and have steadily increased since then, reaching a peak in August. Leaving your keys inside an unlocked vehicle is always a terrible idea, but doing so with a multi-million-dollar hypercar is a uniquely expensive gamble. Bugatti Rimac CEO Mate Rimac recently learned this lesson the hard way after a rather brazen car thief managed to steal his personal Bugatti Chiron directly from a company facility in Croatia. The incident unfolded casually, with security footage showing the suspect smoking a cigarette before wandering into the building, spotting the keys sitting inside the seven-figure machine, and simply driving off.

According to Rimac, he had developed a habit of leaving the keys inside his vehicles, perhaps to avoid the hassle of getting locked out. He likely assumed no one would be foolish enough to steal something so recognizable. Fortunately, an eagle-eyed employee quickly spotted the 1,479-horsepower hypercar speeding away from the factory and immediately alerted the rest of the team through a company group chat, confirming that an unauthorized joyride was indeed in progress.

We caught the drama as it happened on his Instagram page. Rather than simply sitting around and waiting for the authorities to handle the situation, the Bugatti CEO took matters into his own hands. Rimac immediately jumped behind the wheel of a nearby Porsche 911 that fortunately had a full tank of gas and began chasing down the suspect. While the thief already had roughly an hour head start and was actively fleeing toward Slovenia, Rimac had a massive technological advantage: the Chiron’s advanced live telemetry system.

This built-in factory software allowed Rimac and his engineering team to monitor the hypercar’s location, vehicle speed, and exact fuel level in real time. They continuously relayed these live updates to the police via their group chat, effectively turning the stolen Bugatti into an incredibly expensive tracking device. We wonder whether the stolen vehicle was Rimac’s notoriously high-mileage Chiron, though the executive was just relieved the situation remained under digital surveillance as the chase crossed international borders.

The cross-country pursuit finally came to an end after the thief crossed into Austria. The suspect had even stopped to put roughly half a tank of gas into the thirsty quad-turbo, 8.0-liter W16 engine, and naturally, he drove off without paying the fuel bill. Thanks to the constant barrage of live telemetry updates provided by Rimac’s team, Austrian police were eventually able to seamlessly intercept the stolen hypercar.

Fortunately, the Chiron only sustained very minor front bumper damage, avoiding the catastrophic wreckage that easily could have occurred. While I’m sure he must be glad it wasn’t his dream car, a V10-swapped BMW E30, the multi-million-dollar scare prompted an immediate policy change. The CEO has officially vowed to never leave keys inside his vehicles again, putting an end to his trusting factory habits.

#4531. BMW Employs Professional Sniffers to Eliminate New Car Smell

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

BMW’s odor specialists sniff everything from leather to adhesives, and the goal isn’t a pleasant fragrance. It’s a neutral cabin.

Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol Ditches Roof and Luxury for Serious Off-Roading

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

Inside Doug DeMuro's Secret Underground Car Garage

McLaren's Manual V8 McL 6GT Makes Its Public Debut in Las Vegas

That “new car smell” you love is actually a cocktail of chemicals, and BMW has a team of trained sniffers working to get rid of it. Why? It’s because that new-car smell comes from volatile organic compounds evaporating out of hundreds of synthetic parts in a freshly delivered vehicle.

According to BMWBlog, the automaker’s “nose team” works alongside specialized labs to judge how cabin materials really smell. Odor labs have operated in Munich since 1999 and in Shenyang, China, since 2014. Materials go into heated chambers that mimic a hot cabin, and the air is analyzed for compounds, then judged by evaluators against reference standards. The checks come in three stages: single materials, larger parts such as seats and headliners, and finally the complete vehicle, since materials can smell different in combination, especially as temperatures rise. Nils Hesse, BMW’s VP of Product Sustainability, put it this way: “A car doesn’t exist in a lab, but with its occupants.”

Unless you’re buying a BMW, it means nothing. But the science is interesting, and it claims that heat is the enemy. According to the working theory, summer sun raises cabin emissions, while overnight winter parking lowers them. BMW says newer microfiber materials cut emissions and avoid animal-derived proteins, which can cause odor as natural leather ages. Personally, I drive a W123 Mercedes, and the smell of old animal biologics in the upholstery is what sets the scene. In epic contrast, the Neue Klasse iX3 also gets a multi-stage Nano Filter to make sure you’re really only breathing the cleanest, crispest, and most premium air. As for the rest of us, if your car has a smell today, the usual advice applies: crack the windows and park in the shade. If you follow this advice with a new car, the compounds fade by roughly 20 percent a week, so the smell eases over the first few months.

Some of those compounds, like benzene and formaldehyde, are classified as human carcinogens, though typical cabin levels aren’t considered a serious hazard. The U.S. has no federal rules for in-car air, while China requires chemical tests before sale. BMW’s pitch to new car buyers is that a cabin that smells like nothing is a cabin that’s working.

Analysts were looking for about $2.02 billion in revenue, an adjusted loss of $0.61 per share, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of roughly $576 million, according to Bloomberg consensus. Rivian beat all three.

The demand signals for the R2 are good. Rivian says reservation conversion for the launch edition trim stayed above its expectations, it added a second R2 production shift in Normal, Illinois, and demo drives jumped to over 103,000 in the quarter, up from 57,000 in Q2.

The problem is the automotive gross margin. Rivian’s automotive segment posted an $80 million gross loss in Q3, a -5% margin. That’s better than the $130 million loss a year ago, but worse than the $36 million loss (-3%) we saw in Q2.

Rivian blames about $120 million of extra cost of revenue on the R2 ramp, compared to production at “more normalized levels.” And the quarter got help that won’t repeat on demand: $81 million in regulatory credit revenue and an IEEPA tariff refund receivable.

Strip out the credits and the automotive segment lost about $161 million at the gross level, or roughly $8,400 per vehicle delivered. Not great.

But there’s real progress under that. Rivian says automotive cost of goods sold per unit fell by more than $12,000 quarter-over-quarter thanks to the higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage. Our own math from the filing puts it at about $84,700 per vehicle in Q3, down from $96,700 in Q2. Revenue per vehicle is coming down too, which is the point of a cheaper car: about $76,300 excluding credits, versus $85,000 in Q2.

The only reason Rivian posted a consolidated gross profit is its software and services segment, which brought in $605 million in revenue and $256 million in gross profit, a 42% margin.

Of that segment revenue, $354 million (59%) came from the joint venture with Volkswagen Group, which pays Rivian for electrical architecture and software development work. Rivian says it expects to recognize that revenue through about mid-2028. Autonomy+, the paid driver-assist package launched in April, is also in there, and Rivian says take rates are “trending ahead of our expectations.”

With 41,807 deliveries through September, Rivian needs between 25,193 and 28,193 in Q4 to land in the new range. That would be another record by a wide margin. Rivian is providing this guidance a month into the quarter, which gives strong confidence it will hit at leat the lower end of that target.

The capex cut is about “timing of spend,” not savings. Phase 1 of the Georgia plant, which is supposed to add 300,000 units of annual capacity for R2 and R3, is still under construction.

On cash, Rivian ended the quarter with $5.502 billion, or $7.095 billion in total liquidity once you add its credit facility and the $1 billion term loan Volkswagen funded in October. That’s after the $1.5 billion share sale in July. Free cash flow was -$1.124 billion in Q3 alone.

This is a good quarter for Rivian, and the R2 is clearly working. Becoming the best-selling Rivian within one full quarter, while the ramp is still early, is about as good a start as you could ask for. We saw the R2 roll off the line in April, and the demand side has held up since.

But be careful with the headline beat. A lot of it came from outside the car business: Volkswagen’s checks, regulatory credits, and a one-time tariff refund. The thing Rivian actually builds and sells lost more money at the gross level than it did last quarter.

Picked my R2 up a week ago and I’m already in love. It was worth the two year wait! I find myself looking for excuses to jump in and go for a joy ride.

Rivian is going to sell a metric ton of the lower cost versions.

The number we care about most is the $12,000 drop in cost per vehicle. If that keeps going as the second shift fills and the $120 million in ramp costs fade, the automotive segment can get to breakeven on its own. If it stalls, Rivian is a software contractor for VW with a money-losing car company attached.

I am betting on the former. With a shift added right before the quarter started, production will likely increase significantly in Q4, and Rivian already has strong visibility into demand a month into the quarter.

If anything, I’m impressed by the demand Rivian is seeing for the more expensive launch edition of the R2. It bodes well for the cheaper version, as long as it manages to get its cost down over the coming months.

#4529. Yamaha Pulls Out of MotoGP Qatar Due to Safety Risks

Will Yamaha stand alone, or is it just the first domino to fall?

With MotoGP still scheduled to race in Qatar next week amidst the current unrest in the region, Yamaha becomes the first team to pull out of the race.

In a statement delivered by the team on Sunday at the Malaysian Grand Prix, the Japanese manufacturer announced that it would not travel to or compete at the Lusail circuit next week.

Currently, Yamaha as a brand is not allowing any travel in and out of the Middle East, a stance that will not be changed with the continuation of next weekend’s Grand Prix.

“Following its latest assessment of the situation in the Middle East, Yamaha has not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions,” the statement read.

“As a result, Yamaha has informed MotoGP Group about its decision not to participate in the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix.

This decision reflects Yamaha’s assessment of the information currently available and is independent of the measures implemented by MotoGP Group and the event organizer.

Yamaha remains fully committed to MotoGP and looks forward to returning to competition at the Portuguese Grand Prix.”

Currently, Monster Energy Yamaha’s riders Fabio Quartararo and Alex Rins sit 14th and 20th in the standings, as Prima Pramac Yamaha’s Jack Miller sits 19th.

MotoGP replied that they’re disappointed in the decision as they believe that the decision does not take into account the extensive assurances that MotoGP is making to all championship stakeholders.

MotoGP believes its consultations with the State of Qatar, Lusail International Circuit, and independent safety advisors, paired with its own risk assessment process, provide enough certainty.

“MotoGP is disappointed by Yamaha's decision not to participate in the Qatar Grand Prix,” the full statement reads. “While we [recognize] the team is subject to a broader corporate policy restricting travel to the Middle East, we do not believe this decision reflects the extensive assurances provided to all championship stakeholders.

“Following consultation with the State of Qatar, Lusail International Circuit, independent safety advisers and MotoGP's own ongoing risk assessment process, MotoGP has not received any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event.

“We communicated that position, together with the latest available information, to all Manufacturers and Teams today and welcome the confirmation from the remainder of the grid that they will compete in Qatar, and we thank them for that commitment.

“In addition to the contractual implications of Yamaha's decision for its agreements with MotoGP and IRTA, Yamaha's non-participation also carries sporting implications, with any sporting consequences to be managed by the FIM in accordance with the Championship regulations.”

This decision comes as F1 continues to hold back its decision on whether to run what is scheduled to be its penultimate race next month at Lusail.

The ACO has already moved the Dakar Rally out of neighboring Saudi Arabia in January.

#4528. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

America’s EV market has progressed in recent years, but convincing traditional car buyers to switch remains a challenge.

2027 Mazda3 Still Starts Under $25,000, Manual Hatchback Survives

The Original Acura NSX Is Getting Thousands Of New Parts In The U.S.

BYD's Yangwang U9 Extreme Wrecked During Suspected 310 MPH Test Run

Ford Gives a 1966 Mustang a 360-HP V8 and Five-Speed Manual

America’s EV market has made progress, but convincing traditional car buyers to switch remains difficult. As we’ve discussed before, electrification depends on more than adding vehicles to dealership lots. Charging access, affordability, and consumer confidence also shape demand.

A study from HERE Technologies and SBD Automotive puts that challenge into perspective. Its extensive report found that just 11% of surveyed US owners of gasoline and diesel vehicles consider an EV as their most likely next purchase or lease. The result suggests that growing infrastructure and wider model availability have yet to translate into strong buying intent.

The study surveyed 4,058 drivers across eight markets and found a difference between current EV owners and people who have not made the switch. In the US, 85% of EV owners rate charging coverage as good or very good, up from 72% in 2025. That is the highest satisfaction figure among the surveyed markets.

Only 42% of non-EV owners give charging coverage a positive rating. The 43-point gap suggests that direct experience may make drivers more comfortable with the network than they were beforehand.

And that’s despite the massive infrastructure progress we’ve seen this year. US public charging points grew by more than 14% between 2025 and 2026, while average charger power increased from 65kW to 83kW, a 28% rise.

In terms of costs, well, that’s a different problem. Just 34% of US respondents believe EVs are cheaper to own than gasoline-powered vehicles. Another 29% say costs are about the same, while 28% consider EVs more expensive.

There is a brighter picture among people who already own electric cars: 77% of US EV owners say they are likely to buy another one. The report also pointed out that the end of purchase incentives in late 2025 contributed to dampened EV sales into 2026.

Automakers have two jobs: keep current EV owners happy, and somehow win over the skeptics who still worry about price, charging, and whether an EV fits their daily grind. Sure, faster chargers and more plugs make life easier for EV owners, but that doesn’t mean gas-car drivers are suddenly sold. Carmakers still need to prove EVs make sense for the wallet and won’t mess up anyone’s routine.

Right now, America’s EV market has a first-timer problem. Existing owners are mostly on board for round two, but getting more gas-car drivers to take the plunge is still the real challenge.

Ostensibly a mid-size four-door pickup truck, the Ineos Grenadier Quartermaster stretches the definition. Based on the stately Grenadier Wagon, the Quartermaster has a slightly stretched wheelbase and, crucially, a five-foot bed (61.5 inches to be precise) where the wagon—and SUV by any other name—has an enclosed cargo area. The mechanicals are nearly identical, the Quartermaster using the same BMW-sourced 281-hp turbocharged inline-six, eight-speed automatic transmission, solid axles, and four-wheel drive system as the wagon. While its retro-Rover styling could be construed as pretentious, its 1840-pound payload capacity and 7716-pound tow rating tell a different story. Yes, the fuel economy is daunting, and the steering remains vague despite some recent updates, but the Quartermaster knows exactly what it is and who it appeals to, and in that sense it’s without fault.

Expert Tip: The Quartermaster's obvious alternative is the Grenadier Station Wagon; but if having a pickup bed on a trail-eating machine is non-negotiable, check out the Jeep Gladiator, which displays a little visual sass of its own while offering similar towing and payload capacities at a lower price.

It includes special saddle leather on the steering wheel, handbrake handle, and passenger grab handle, plus heated Recaro seats, premium floor mats, unique alloy wheels, and a few other upscale additions.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

You won't find another off-roader on the trail with a central nervous system like the Quartermaster's. A turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six from BMW, good for 281 horsepower and 331 pound-feet of torque, mates with an eight-speed automatic transmission and a permanent four-wheel-drive system with a two-speed mechanical transfer case. A locking center differential is standard, but front and rear lockers are also available. Under the body lie two solid axles that are suspended with coil springs at all four corners.

Like the Jeep Gladiator pickup, the Ineos uses recirculating-ball steering rather than a modern rack-and-pinion setup. It takes some getting used to—it feels less precise and requires more corrections—especially if you are familiar with modern electric power steering setups. Think of it as underscoring the vintage feel of this truck.

Despite its financial struggles, Aston Martin continues to produce some remarkable cars, including the Valkyrie, which features a naturally aspirated V12 in an era of engine downsizing, and more recently, the open-top Valhalla, capable of matching the coupe’s 217-mph top speed. However, these engineering achievements haven’t translated into significant financial success, as the British automaker continues to struggle six years after Canadian billionaire Lawrence Stroll led a rescue investment in 2020.

According to Bloomberg, citing Aston Martin’s Q3 2026 financial results, the automaker reported a pretax loss of £77 million ($102 million), narrowing from £111.9 million ($148 million) a year earlier. Its net loss also fell from £131.8 million ($175 million) to £78.8 million ($104 million). Despite the improvement, the company’s net debt reached £1.57 billion ($2.1 billion), while cumulative after-tax losses since Stroll’s takeover have reached £2.3 billion ($3.1 billion).

Interestingly, Aston Martin’s wholesale deliveries remained virtually unchanged at 1,431 vehicles in Q3 2026, compared with 1,430 a year earlier. Still, revenue increased 36% to £389 million ($515 million), while gross profit jumped 76%. This improvement reflects a richer sales mix.

The improvements are partly driven by the Valhalla, the brand’s first PHEV supercar, rivaling the likes of the Ferrari 849 Testarossa and Lamborghini Revuelto. The Valhalla was initially capped at 999 examples, although combined coupe and Spider production is now expected to slightly exceed that figure. Such exclusive, high-priced models could help improve profitability, a strategy that has also worked for luxury brands like Rolls-Royce.

The new Valhalla Spider is expected to cost about 20% more than the coupe, which could further help profitability. There’s also the Valen, another limited-series model touted as the world’s most powerful front-engined production car. Arriving in Q2 2027, the Valen comes with a 5.2-liter twin-turbocharged V12 producing 838 horsepower, about 19 hp more than the Ferrari 12Cilindri, though the Ferrari supercar retains a naturally aspirated setup.

It remains to be seen how Aston Martin’s upcoming models and improving financial performance will help the automaker overcome its mounting debt and return to profitability. The company continues to face challenges, including weaker demand in China, U.S. tariffs, and more recently, legal challenges from bondholders such as Arini Capital over its financing arrangements.

Beyond production cars, Stroll has also been investing heavily in Formula 1, where the Aston Martin team, which operates separately from the road-car company, serves as a global marketing platform for the luxury brand. The team has also partnered with Honda as its exclusive power unit supplier since the start of the 2026 season, a collaboration that could eventually lead to a jointly developed road car.

#4522. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

#4521. McLaren Confirms Next Supercar Will Be Called McL 820 and Have 809 HP

The successor to the outgoing 750S will hit the streets and racetracks sometime in 2027.

Earlier this month, McLaren told the world that the 750S supercar will end production sometime next year. Naturally, we wondered what will come next. While there’s still a lot we have to learn, McLaren today confirmed the name of the successor to the 750S as well as its horsepower rating.

The McL 820 will be McLaren’s next supercar. The name was initially teased on a giant kiwi statue (pictured below) that the automaker unveiled in central London, with its body wearing a camouflage wrap featuring the “McL 820” name. For anyone who is confused about why McLaren chose a flightless bird endemic to New Zealand as its mascot, the company’s founder, Bruce McLaren, is from that country and originally used the kiwi as a visual centerpiece for his racing team’s branding.

See all results for used McLaren for sale near 29617

Like with McLaren’s previous model names, the numeric designation represents their output in metric horsepower (a.k.a. PS). That continues with the McL 820, with 820 PS converting to 809 mechanical horsepower. That’s a considerable uptick versus its predecessor, with the standard 750S making 740 horses. The “McL” prefix is also new for the company’s production cars, though it was previewed on the McL 6GT that was revealed during this year’s Monterey Car Week. McLaren says its next supercar will mark the start of a new naming convention that incorporates McL.

There’s obviously still a lot of mystery surrounding the forthcoming McL 820, but McLaren says that information will start to be revealed next year, with the car itself also slated to hit the streets and racetracks sometime in 2027.

#4520. The Nissan Frontier Ronin Concept Is a Proper Ford Ranger Raptor Fighter

Twin-turbo power, bucket seats, and 35-inch tires make this Frontier concept look all but unstoppable.

The Nissan Frontier has been a workhorse truck for the Japanese brand, but now the industrious pickup is ready to have some fun. For the 2026 Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show, Nissan built the Frontier Ronin Concept, a proper high-speed off-road truck with the right proportions and hardware.

Nissan says the Ronin name means “masterless warrior” in Japanese [A fact that every true car enthusiast should know, because of the movie by the same name that contains some of cinema’s greatest car chases —Ed.] and represents the truck’s fearless personality. But the real excitement starts under the hood of this Frontier concept.

Nissan swapped out the typical naturally aspirated V-6 for a twin-turbocharged version of the 3.8-liter VQ38DD six-pot. This twin-turbo setup isn’t a simple plug-and-play version, either; Nissan used a rear-mounted R35 GT-R Nismo twin-turbo system with ECUTEK engine management, a dual off-road air intake system, and a custom exhaust system to soup it up even further. Power figures weren’t provided, but we can probably assume this truck makes a healthy amount of power.

A custom Titan Suspension system increases track width by a whopping 12 inches and ride height by four inches. Bespoke Bilstein Black Hawk high-performance suspension adds four-way adjustment, plus individual high- and low-speed compression, rebound, and bypass damping. In total, the Frontier Ronin concept features 14 inches of suspension travel. Custom control arms, spindles, and axles are also present to round things out between wheels and body.

SEMA Show often offers a glimpse at technology that automakers are prototyping or ideas they’re considering for production, and Nissan is showing off a set of prototype 17-inch beadlock wheels wrapped in 35-inch Yokohama Geolandar all-terrain tires on the Frontier concept, which give the truck a mean stance. A custom high-performance big brake kit with six-piston front calipers and two-piece floating rotors sits inside.

The interior is far from stock, too. Kinetic sport bucket seats, custom topographic-inspired seat belts, and a triple dashboard gauge pod with boost, oil pressure, & exhaust temp make up the primary interior upgrades. Outside, Nissan added a new front fascia and grille, custom high-clearance bumpers, wider fender flares, and a front skid plate. Plus, the carmaker installed a whole host of Nismo Off-Road accessories—including rock sliders, a roof rack, and pillar lights.

Of course, this build will likely not go into production, as much as we would love to have it battle the Ford Ranger Raptor, Chevrolet Colorado ZR2 Bison, and Toyota Tacoma TRD Pro. SEMA builds represent what is possible, but isn’t usually pragmatic, for automakers. Even so, this kind of Frontier is exactly the kind of truck we’d like to see ripping around Baja.

#4519. BYD spotted testing a new minivan [Video]

BYD’s upcoming multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) was spotted on a car carrier and at one of its Flash Charging stations ahead of its expected debut later this year.

Spy images of BYD’s new Ocean MPV testing in China have begun flooding the internet over the past few days.

BYD first unveiled the Ocean-V concept at the 2026 Beijing Auto Show in April, a futuristic preview of its first MPV under the Ocean series.

The concept featured a sliding center display screen and two unique modes: Camping and Movie. In camping mode, the seats either fold flat to create a bed or swivel to face each other.

Movie mode, on the other hand, transforms the vehicle into a private mobile theater with a large display screen that flips out of the dashboard.

With exciting features and a futuristic design, many couldn’t wait to see what the production version would look like.

The prototype spotted in testing is a bit disappointing. Although it’s still disguised, the image from Autohome shows a vehicle that looks very different from the Ocean-V concept earlier this year.

The image shows a boxy design with a wide grille and traditional pull-style door handles, which looks drastically different from BYD’s latest vehicles.

Spotted at a BYD Flash Charger in China, the vehicle was equipped with a massive roof-mounted LiDAR. A video (shown below) of the new model on a car carrier from ThinkerCar offers a closer look.

Local reports suggest the Ocean MPV will be 5,145 mm long, 1,970 mm wide, and 1,805 mm tall, with a 3,045 mm wheelbase. It’s also expected to feature a 2+2+3 seating layout with room for seven passengers.

A video has just surfaced of a BYD Ocean MPV test mule. It’s still heavily camouflaged, with the exterior looking largely identical to conventional MPVs. The real question is whether the interior brings something novel. https://t.co/WydRv1jiGf pic.twitter.com/aKzOtHMJKa

BYD’s current MPV lineup includes the Denza D9, a flagship model that starts above 300,000 yuan ($45,000), and the Xia, priced in the 200,000 to 300,000 yuan ($30,000 to $45,000) range. The Ocean MPV is expected to fill the gap.

Zhang Zhou, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series, said the company expects to launch its first MPV by the end of 2026.

For over 30 years, Ferrari has been letting its customers race its cars in one-make championships. It started in 1993 with the 348, first around Europe, then with a North American series, and later in other parts of the world.

The cars have changed a lot since then. The 348 Challenge became the F355 Challenge, and its successors have become the go-to for the racing series. But in 2003, Ferrari thought it would be a good idea to sell road-going versions of the race cars to even more customers who’d like the experience without having to enter the championship series.

The result was the 360 Challenge Stradale, effectively a road-legal version of the actual race car. At the time, it was matched up against the 911 GT3 RS of the 996.2 generation, and it made for very interesting comparisons. But while Porsche continued building stripped-out, lightweight road-legal racing 911s, Ferrari did not.

But after more than 20 years, Ferrari is bringing back the 296 Challenge Stradale. Like many of 360 Challenge Stradale, it’s taking about four years to get it done, but it’s reportedly coming before the end of the year. That’s according to The Supercar Blog, and that’s not the only bit of information that the publication managed to obtain.

Previously, it was said that the 296 Challenge Stradale would debut sometime in November. Now, a date appears to have been locked in, and it’s slated to premiere during Finali Mondiali at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya. If so, it’s a fitting way to end the 2026 Ferrari Challenge season, which will be held from November 17 to 23. Ferrari will pull the covers off the car on the 21st, and prices are said to start at €320,000 or around $358,000.

The first Challenge Stradale model in over 20 years was first spied back in February. The camouflaged prototype was seen driving around the streets of Maranello, sporting a unique aero package that also includes a whopper of a rear wing among other things.

It’s said that the car won’t have the standard 296’s plug-in hybrid system. If true, that means it’ll be exactly like the 296 Challenge that has been running around the world’s circuits for about three years now. For power, we can expect around 690 hp, which is far less than the hybrid model; the removal of the electrified bits does mean it’s over 300 lbs lighter at the very least. Of course, the Stradale will have some creature comforts, but we’re expecting it to weigh closer to 3,000 lbs. For comparison, the hybrid coupe tips the scales at over 3,500 lbs.

Of course, Ferrari can eke out more horses out of its twin-turbo V6 to make up the difference for losing the electric boost. It’s been rumored that it’ll have about 720 hp, which actually makes it more powerful than the race car. Of course, the race car is a far lighter vehicle, but that’s not to say the Stradale will be a blunt instrument. Mind you, Ferrari may have a couple more track-focused cars coming soon, and 2027 might just be an exciting year for the Prancing Horse.

#4517. These Are Our Top-Rated Car Brands, Ranked

We averaged the individual ratings of the hundreds of models on sale to determine which brands are top-rated overall in our evaluations.

Which brands make the best cars? It's an age-old question that's constantly changing as car companies compete with each other to produce the latest and greatest products. But it's a question that we set out to answer with our comprehensive testing of every new vehicle we can get our hands on. We rate vehicle models on a one-to-10 scale—find more about how we determine our ratings here—and now we've averaged all our ratings by brand to determine which ones earn the highest ratings in Car and Driver's testing. We included the top 10 brands in this list.

Because we rate vehicles within their relative segments, this ranking of car brands shows which makes produce the most competitive products across the industry. These ratings come from a combination of objective instrumented testing and subjective real-world driving experience. And note that our ratings are constantly changing as we evaluate new products, so these average scores merely represent a snapshot of where these brands stand in today's evaluations.

Lucid is a new electric automaker that only started selling cars a few years ago, but it's off to a strong start. Both the Lucid Air electric luxury sedan and Lucid Gravity electric luxury SUV are previous winners of our 10Best award, so it's no surprise they rate highly in our book.

Porsche's lineup used to consist of only sports cars, but it has expanded in the past few decades to include SUVs, sedans, and several electric models. With the 911 sports car serving as the cornerstone of Porsche's excellent driving dynamics, the brand does a good job infusing the same precise feel into its other products, so nearly all Porsche models carry high C/D ratings.

Rivian, like Lucid, is a new EV automaker that has only a few models in its stable. But they're all good at what they do, so it's one of our top-rated brands. The R1S SUV and R1T pickup truck are Rivian's larger offerings, and the R2 compact SUV arrived recently to bring the brand's entry price point down to a more accessible level.

Another relatively new brand that quickly rose to the upper echlons of the automotive world is Genesis, Hyundai's luxury spinoff. It's been around since 2015, and its products have improved rapidly. The GV70 and GV80 luxury SUVs both sit near the top of their class, while the G70, G80, and G90 sedans are also strong offerings, bolstering Genesis' average score above its more well-established luxury competitors in our ratings.

Honda models regularly earn multiple spots on our annual list of 10Best award winners, so it's no surprise that this brand places highly here. The mainstream Accord, Civic, and CR-V comprise the core of the Honda lineup in terms of sales, but there's excellence to be found elsewhere, such as the Passport two-row SUV and the high-performance Si and Type R variants of the Civic.

Volkswagen may have shifted its focus towards SUVs in the U.S., but it still offers enthusiast favorites including the Golf GTI and Golf R that help bolster its reputation among car lovers. Plus, its SUV offerings are competitive, especially the Tiguan which places highly in our compact-SUV rankings.

BMW has a broad lineup ranging from small sedans to full-size, three-row SUVs. And there's a clear throughline within this portfolio, as most BMW models are competitive in their segments and offer the satisfying driving dynamics and refined powertrains we've come to expect from this German luxury marque.

Familiar Ford nameplates such as the Focus and Fusion have been gone for years now, as the Blue Oval now builds almost exclusively SUVs and trucks. But its SUVs and trucks are largely competitive, and there's plenty of fun to be had within the Bronco side of the corral. And of course, the Mustang pony car is still going strong.

Hyundai has an impressively full lineup of sedans, SUVs, and even a pickup truck, and it's taken the fight to stalwarts such as Honda and Toyota by offering many hybrid and battery-electric models in competitive segments. The Palisade Hybrid SUV and Ioniq 5 electric SUV are among the brand's current standout models.

Mazda earned its way into our hearts by building the MX-5 Miata sports car—and then by imbuing its more mainstream sedans and SUVs with the same fun-to-drive spirit. Some newer Mazdas have prioritized technology and size over driving enjoyment, so a few models have slipped in our ratings, but the brand still offers several models sitting at or near the top of their segments.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine. He has been part of the Hearst Autos team since 2016 and now lives in New York City.
