#4448. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

As long as it is just providing information, it won't. However, what will be significant here is who gets the information. This could significantly limit the ability of bike thieves to resell stolen e-bikes or e-bike batteries.

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4447. Rivian's Charging Network Grew 39% In A Year

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Rivian’s Adventure Network of DC fast chargers has expanded nearly 40% in the last 12 months, surpassing 1,100 individual chargers and 150 locations across the United States.

The company said in its third-quarter earnings report that its EV fast charging network now has 1,185 ports capable of delivering up to 300 kilowatts of power, up 39% compared to last year’s third quarter. Meanwhile, the number of stations has gone up to 165, or 26% more than at the end of Q3 2025.

The startup claims its fast chargers are powered by 100% renewable energy, though that doesn’t always mean that he electricity coming out of a charger is sourced from a photovoltaic array or a wind farm. Instead, every kilowatt-hour delivered through a RAN charger is matched with renewable sources that may operate in another town or another state.

Rivian has continued to invest in its own charging infrastructure, which uses purpose-built stalls, even though its passenger models have access to tens of thousands of public DC chargers across the U.S., including countless NACS-equipped Tesla Superchargers.

However, while the DC charging infrastructure was mentioned in the startup’s latest presentation, the Waypoints network of Level 2 chargers has gotten a lot less attention. The slower chargers didn’t get a single mention in any of the company’s most recent documents, but they haven’t been completely forgotten.

That said, the growth rate seems to have been significantly slower compared to the RAN network. According to data from the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC), the company installed just ten 11-kilowatt chargers this year, with the latest pair going online in October. In total, Rivian operates 540 Waypoint Level 2 chargers at 208 locations in the U.S.

Despite the quick growth in its DC charging network, the California startup is still a tiny player in a rapidly evolving industry. By comparison, Tesla, the biggest name in the game, has over 40,000 fast charging ports at nearly 3,300 locations in the U.S., with an additional 14,000 Level 2 Destination Chargers at almost 4,000 sites.

#4446. How to Choose the Best Car Battery

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Here's what you need to know to choose the right battery for your vehicle.

We've all experienced the stomach-churning trauma of a dead car battery. You need to be somewhere and you're running late. You jump in, twist the key or push the start button, and . . . nothing! Or maybe just a sickening click-click. Suddenly you need a jump-start or, worse, a tow. And probably a new battery, too. But which one?

So many brands, types, prices, and places to buy them. Which to choose and why? You don't need to be an expert to make an informed, cost-efficient purchase. Here are some brands we trust, but always check your owner’s manual for details and recommendations.

Check your owner's manual for your original battery's size, specifications, and ratings. You can also find which one you need from guides in the auto-parts store or online.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

Replacing a battery yourself is an option; it's not particularly difficult. Some shops offer free installation—but only if the battery is purchased from them.

If you're buying one of the batteries above online and installing it yourself, be sure to check your owner's manual for critical information before purchasing your new battery. Modern cars have specific requirements on their electrical systems, and the wrong power source could leave you stranded.

Most batteries are located up front, under the hood, where they're easy to access and replace with a couple of wrenches. But some are buried in the trunk or elsewhere—not so easy to find, let alone remove and replace.

Just remember, the negative terminal is always the first thing you disconnect and the last thing you reconnect.

Regardless of whether you're doing it in your driveway or letting a shop install, it's a good idea to first make sure you're buying the correct physical size. A number of sizes fit today's wide variety of vehicles.

For instance, size 24/24F (top terminal) batteries fit many Honda, Acura, Toyota, Lexus, Nissan, and Infiniti vehicles, while size 35 (top terminal) units fit many other Japanese vehicles, including recent Toyotas, Nissans, Hondas, and Subarus.

Size 48H6 (top terminal) batteries fit many European and American vehicles. Again, you can find which size you need in your owner's manual, in the replacement guides at the retail store, or online.

Almost all cars come with a 12-volt sealed lead-acid (SLA) battery of some variety (a few high-performance cars are equipped with lithium-ion batteries). These SLA batteries use the same chemistry as the ones your dad had to periodically top off with water, but today they are sealed—hence the name—and maintenance-free.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

Absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries have quickly become the norm for most modern cars. They use similar chemistry as SLAs but are more durable and are claimed to stand up to more charge cycles.

Gel-cell batteries are best for deep discharging but may have problems in extreme hot or cold. Those old "wet cell" batteries from Dad's day are still available, though primarily for older models or penny pinchers. They are likely not offered in the right sizes and specs to support modern cars, however.

The next thing to check is the engine-cranking power of a vehicle battery, which is expressed in cranking amps (CA) and/or cold-cranking amps (CCA), a measure of how much electric current (in amperes) it can deliver for 30 seconds at 32 and zero degrees Fahrenheit. A bigger number is better, especially in cold weather, when batteries are at their weakest.

Another number to understand is the battery's reserve capacity, which is how long it can provide power with the engine off and headlights and/or accessories on or if the vehicle's charging system fails. One and a half hours is good. Two hours is better.

Also important is the warranty, which should be at least three years for full replacement (assuming no signs of neglect or abuse), plus, in some cases, a prorated refund for some time after that. Bear in mind, manufacturer warranties are often not supported when parts and accessories are purchased online from retailers like Amazon or Walmart.

Finally, be forewarned: Some brands, such as BMW, require the battery to be "coded" (digitally mated) to the car or it will not take a charge. Coding the battery requires BMW-specific OBD-II software that any reputable service shop or BMW dealer will have.

Expect to pay anywhere between $100 and $400 for a new battery, with lower-performing SLA types at the low end and stronger, longer-lasting AGMs near the top. If you're having it installed, the shop will dispose of your old battery.

If you're doing it yourself, take your old one to the retail outlet for recycling and to avoid a core charge—a mandatory deposit on your new battery that is refunded when you return the old one. Before you hand it over, place it side by side with the new battery to confirm the one you're buying is the same size. It's a final check to make sure your choice is the right one.

Oh, and if you're taking it home to install, get one with a traveling handle if possible—a car battery can weigh between 25 and 60 pounds.

Ford and Chevrolet may be the most recognized brands in the American racing scene, but Ferrari once considered joining the fray. In the 1980s, company founder Enzo Ferrari was frustrated with Formula 1 politics and proposed regulation changes, and threatened to leave the sport. He commissioned the Ferrari 637 in 1986 for a potential entry into the CART Indy Car World Series and the Indy 500, but it never entered a race.

There was another vehicle that came out of that unusual chapter of the Prancing Horse brand’s history, which led CART entrants on the track. Well, the vehicle in question is a one-off Ferrari Mondial designed to serve as a pace car. A recent video uploaded by AVANTS on YouTube brought the pace car, now part of The Caretakers Collection, back into the spotlight, sharing some interesting bits about an American venture that never fully materialized.

The Ferrari Mondial pace car was part of the PPG Pace Car program, which fielded different vehicles at CART events, including a 1983 Dodge Daytona Turbo Z and a 1992 Subaru SVX. While the Mondial wasn’t as celebrated as Ferrari models like the Testarossa, this particular pace car has some interesting provenance.

For one, the Ferrari pace car reportedly cost $1 million to build in 1987, which, adjusted to today’s money, is around $3 million. Designed by Italian firm I.DE.A Institute, the pace car came with an extended wheelbase, redesigned front and rear bodywork, and, of course, integrated warning lights. It also featured a brake-cooling system that sprayed water through nozzles. The cabin, meanwhile, featured a custom dashboard and steering wheel, along with Kevlar and suede accents.

Powering the PPG project was an experimental 3.4-liter V8 producing a reported 300 horsepower. Forza Magazine said that the engine was being developed for the upcoming Ferrari 348. So, aside from just leading the field, the pace car also served as an early showcase for the automaker’s upcoming powertrain technology.

This Ferrari Mondial pace car isn’t for sale. But it offers a glimpse into a lesser-known era of the Italian marque’s history, especially considering the brand is better known for its strong presence in F1.

Today, the IndyCar Series uses different pace cars depending on the event, with the 2026 Indy 500 paced by the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X. In F1, the duties of the pace car, better known as the safety car, are handled by the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+.

Average gas car lasts ~150k miles. For sure requiring more maintenance to reach that mileage than an EV. Achieving ~500k on the original motor and over 300k on a battery is quite impressive.

Getting towards the 100k mile mark in both our EVs. Both feel like brand new and have required almost no maintenance - a fraction of what would be required with ICE. #4443. VW’s EV Factory Is Now Taking Cars Apart. There’s Money In It

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen has spent years converting its Zwickau factory to build electric cars, and now only electric cars roll off its production lines. But now it has received a new assignment: taking cars apart. The German plant has opened an industrial dismantling line, adding a new revenue stream.

Zwickau became VW’s electric manufacturing hub through a €1.2 billion conversion that began in 2018. ID.3 production started in November 2019, the last combustion car followed in June 2020, and the transformation was completed in January 2022 with the ID.5. Retooled production lines, extra automation, and extensive employee training now enable the factory to build six MEB-based EVs for Volkswagen, Audi, and Cupra.

The new eight-stage dismantling line will initially handle preproduction vehicles, but will eventually also handle cars at the end of their life. From 2027, it will process 4,100 vehicles annually across two shifts, employing 100 workers who were retrained for the new role. Construction and approvals took nine months, finishing three months early; VW says it could reuse manufacturing equipment to cut costs.

The automaker says it has been selling usable original parts recovered at Zwickau since July, with doors, bumpers, motors and transmission components reportedly in especially high demand. They’re available through its dealer and service networks, independent workshops and parts retailers.

The idea is to make repairs affordable enough to keep older cars on the road instead of writing them off. The dismantling line initially handles pre-production vehicles, although VW doesn’t identify which cars supplied the parts already sold. It also hasn’t disclosed prices, sales volumes, warranty terms, or how it inspects components before resale.

Material recovery is another money-making opportunity. Separating plastics before recycling helps preserve their usefulness for new components. VW says plastic recovered from one vehicle could contribute recycled material to three new cars (not all of it, though).

VW is also looking to expand its recycling business and plans to invest up to €90 million, with the Saxony government pledging €10.7 million, and it could eventually support 1,000 jobs. Zwickau has no vehicle production planned beyond 2031, though, so this new recycling line still leaves its long-term future uncertain.

That uncertainty comes as Volkswagen’s rising EV sales are putting pressure on its profit margins, because its electric models still earn less than combustion cars. The squeeze has also prompted it to pause development of the upcoming electric Golf until it can accommodate the investment. For now, dismantling remains a business whose profitability at scale needs proving, and it’s unclear if this can generate enough work (and profit) to really matter for the Zwickau plant.

VW hasn't said the operation will be limited to EVs, though, and the photos it published seem to suggest otherwise. At least one of the cars pictured (the dark blue one) appears to be a Golf, although the captions don’t identify the models. Zwickau may build only electric cars, but its new used parts business looks set to cater to a broader crowd to maximize revenue potential.

After revealing a slew of low-slung SEMA concepts last week, including a rad 300-horsepower Sentra SE-R Spec-V, Nissan is turning its attention to something considerably taller. The automaker is bringing three truck and SUV concepts to the 2026 SEMA Show, showcasing different interpretations of off-road capability and customization. One of them is the Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol, which takes the full-size SUV in a rather unconventional direction.

Inspired by rugged Nissan vehicles that have tackled challenging environments worldwide, including the Patrol, the Jungle Patrol concept is designed around the idea of an expedition-ready machine. It trades much of the Armada’s conventional SUV character for an open-air configuration, specialized off-road hardware, and a safari-inspired cabin. The result is a vehicle that looks more suited to exploring remote trails than navigating the school run.

The most noticeable change is the open-roof configuration, which removes the conventional roof in favor of a tubular steel roll cage. Nissan also fitted custom inward-facing bench seats with harnesses, giving the cabin the appearance of a traditional safari vehicle.

Outside, the Armada gets decked out with jungle-themed graphics, beefy tubular steel bumpers, and fender flares that mean business. NISMO Off Road throws in roof-mounted six-inch lights and rock sliders, so you can light up the trail and bash rocks without breaking a sweat.

The concept also gets a substantial suspension upgrade. Its widened track incorporates custom CJD long-travel racing suspension, featuring adjustable high-performance coilovers with remote reservoirs. This setup is paired with prototype NISMO 18-inch AXIS beadlock wheels wrapped in 37×12.50R18 Yokohama Geolandar G003 M/T tires.

Under the hood, the Armada retains its direct-injected 3.5-liter VR35 V6 engine. The standard powerplant produces 425 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque. Nissan adds a prototype NISMO cat-back exhaust system, while Mobil 1 Extended Performance Oil is also included in the build.

The Armada Jungle Patrol is only one of three concepts Nissan prepared for this year’s SEMA Show. Nissan says these concepts are intended to inspire owners to personalize their vehicles while allowing its designers and engineers to gather feedback on potential future accessories and product directions.

The company also pointed toward its upcoming all-new Xterra, suggesting that more capable trucks and SUVs remain part of its future plans. However, none of the three SEMA builds will become production models in their current form – though Nissan says some accessories featured on the concepts may eventually be available through dealerships.

The 2026 SEMA Show runs from November 3 to 6 at the Las Vegas Convention Center in Las Vegas, Nevada. Visitors can find Nissan’s concepts at booth No. 21521 in Central Hall.

#4441. Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.

The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.

That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.

It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.

The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.

It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.

Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.

Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.

Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.

“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.

Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.

While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.

That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.

The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.

As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.

All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.

At $1,399, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.

And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.

The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.

For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.

And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its Black Friday sale.

The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.

So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.

#4440. Polestar 2 Production Is Officially Over. A Successor Is Coming In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The first-generation Polestar 2 is dead for good. Production of the brand’s first electric model has ended in Luqiao, China, a company representative confirmed to InsideEVs after a report from Norway’s TV2 surfaced last month.

After six years in production, Polestar’s first mass-market model sold roughly 200,000 units worldwide and set the stage for what came next. The Polestar 2 competed with the Tesla Model 3, and although it was smaller and more expensive than the American-made electric sedan, it had plenty of fans everywhere. (Healthy lease discounts likely helped.)

The European-spec Polestar 2 got its last facelift last year.

The lovable four-door electric sedan went through several facelifts, including one that significantly changed the way it drives. When the car was introduced in 2000, its base trim was front-wheel drive, and dual-motor all-wheel drive was available as an option. But in 2023, the entry-level models became rear-wheel drive, while the top versions continued to offer AWD.

More power and more range were also added along the way, keeping the CMA-based EV up to date in an increasingly crowded market. At its peak, the Polestar 2 had up to 314 miles of EPA-estimated range, which is plenty for daily use, but ultimately the Tesla Model 3’s lower price made the Swedish-designed EV a tougher sell.

In the United States, the Polestar 2 was discontinued last year, a move that seemed to foreshadow the brand’s demise stateside. While the company’s entry-level model was axed because of hiked import tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, Polestar was ultimately strong-armed to stop selling vehicles here, after a decision from the U.S. Department of Commerce denied the automaker an authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule.

That said, Polestar continues to sell EVs in Europe and other parts of the world, and while the first-generation Polestar 2 has been discontinued globally, a new generation is scheduled to debut next year.

With a design inspired by the Formula 2030 concept, the new Polestar 2 is expected to follow in its predecessor’s footsteps as a mashup between a small sedan and crossover, though the company hasn’t confirmed what lies in store for the new model, design-wise.

The new Polestar 2 is part of the Geely-owned automaker’s plan to launch no fewer than four new models in just three years. Half of that plan has already been enacted, with the Polestar 5 grand tourer and Polestar 4 SUV already going on sale in Europe earlier this year. Next up is the new Polestar 2, followed by a small crossover, the Polestar 7.

#4439. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

The Pontiac GTO is one of those cars everyone knows, and for good reason. It helped kick off the muscle car craze in the ’60s, and its impact is still felt long after the original left the scene.

With a name like that, you just know someone had to give it the restomod treatment. Enter Ringbrothers and their latest wild idea: Billie. This one started out as a humble 1965 Pontiac Tempest Convertible before getting the full transformation.

Ringbrothers, based in Wisconsin, has a reputation for going all-out on their builds. These are the folks behind the 805-hp Aston Martin DBS-based Octavia, just to name one. Now they’ve set their sights on Pontiac muscle, and the result might just be the wildest GTO we’ve seen.

This project ate up more than 5,500 hours, packed with metalwork, fabrication, and some serious engineering wizardry.

The first thing you’ll notice is the bodywork. Ringbrothers stretched the car five inches wider, gave it reshaped front fenders, beefed-up rear quarters, and longer rocker panels. Carbon-fiber doors and a bunch of custom panels round out the look.

Jim Ring says the team obsessed over getting the lines just right, making sure the mods looked natural and not overdone. With a car like the GTO, keeping that classic shape is half the battle.

The whole thing is finished in a custom color called Billie Goat Blue, with shiny chrome and black accents. Custom bumpers, a billet aluminum taillight panel, and a carbon-fiber diffuser with built-in exhausts complete the package.

Inside, it’s just as wild. The dash is pushed four inches forward and dropped two inches for more space up front. You get new aluminum trim, a digital display, and even the original radio reworked with Bluetooth.

One quirky touch: the custom shifter is inspired by an olive wood espresso portafilter. It’s a weird choice, but somehow it works with the hand-built vibe.

Under the hood, there’s a supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8 from Wegner Automotive, good for 650 horsepower and 650 lb-ft. That’s a massive jump over anything the original GTO ever dreamed of. All that power goes through a Bowler 10-speed auto. Ringbrothers even built a custom exhaust with Flowmaster bits, so it sounds as mean as it looks.

Underneath, Billie sits on a Roadster Shop Fast Track Stage III chassis with FOX coilovers and six-piston Brembos. HRE G-Code wheels – 19s up front, 20s out back – are wrapped in sticky Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2s. All this should make Billie handle way better than any stock GTO, especially with all that LT4 muscle under the hood.

If you’re hoping to buy Billie, you’re out of luck – this one’s headed to a private owner after its 2026 SEMA Show debut in Las Vegas. No word on price, but with over 5,500 hours sunk into it, you can bet it wasn’t cheap.

#4437. Rivian Has Invested Millions In 3D Printing. Its Biggest Plans Are Still Ahead

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Additive manufacturing is helping automakers come up with design mock-ups faster and cheaper than ever before, and Rivian is going all in on the technology. The California startup has spent over $5 million on 3D printers, using the machines to build tangible prototypes of various parts significantly faster than going down the traditional route, which involves at least one external supplier and big, expensive stamping equipment.

But Rivian is just getting started. In an interview with CNBC, Jonathan Dankenbring, the startup’s head of additive manufacturing, said that the company doesn’t have a choice but to scale up and begin using it across all factions. “We’re going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company,” Dankenbring said.

So far, the R2’s maker has used 3D printers on a relatively small scale at its facility in Detroit, Michigan. The R2’s steering wheel was first printed using additive manufacturing before becoming a metal part. The technology has also been used to make electric motors for fluid testing, screw guides for tooling, stamping press inserts, and some production parts, like trim pieces, for early builds.

For the next step, Rivian is installing new 3D printers that can build flexible silicone parts. At its factory in Normal, Illinois, where its entire lineup is being assembled, the startup is adding a bay of machines, enabling employees to print parts on demand. “3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible,” said Dankenbring for CNBC.

Besides the $5 million spent on 3D printers, Rivian is also paying roughly $1.7 million for the raw materials used in the machines every year. That’s quite a big sum for something that may look like big toys, but in the end, it makes a lot of financial sense for the EV manufacturer. According to Dankenbring, the cost savings have been “well in the millions” compared to traditional prototyping techniques, but more importantly, 3D printing speeds things up considerably.

By building small batches of parts on-site, the car company can lower its supplier tooling costs, cut logistics expenses, and reduce production times from weeks to days, and sometimes hours.

Rivian isn’t the only car manufacturer that has leaned into additive manufacturing. Tesla, Ford, General Motors, and many others have been using the technology to make stuff faster and cheaper, thanks in large part to the 3D printing industry’s massive advancements.

A decade ago, getting a 3D printer came with an eye-watering bill, but now, anyone can buy a machine for as little as a couple hundred dollars. The printers have also gotten smaller, faster, and more precise, enabling hobbyists and big companies to create bespoke parts in a matter of hours.

Correction: CNBC interviewed Jonathan Dankenbring, not Jared Beck. The article has been updated to reflect this change.

#4436. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4435. Hyundai Says Hydrogen Cars Aren’t Dead. Finding Customers Is Another Story

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Hydrogen fuel cell cars were supposed to be the next leap forward in the automotive world. They drive like electric cars, but you can refuel them with hydrogen and drive hundreds of miles without having to sit at a charger for half an hour, and best of all, there are no nasty emissions.

It sounds like the perfect solution for pretty much everybody. Yet, ask anyone if they know someone who’s driving a hydrogen car, and they’ll struggle to come up with an answer. Toyota tried (and is still trying) with the Mirai, and Hyundai is still trying with the new Nexo. BMW, General Motors, Honda, and others have also dipped their toes into the technology, with varying degrees of success.

The second-generation Hyundai Nexo FCEV was unveiled in 2025, when it was touted as a global model.

But why aren’t we all driving FCEVs? For starters, there’s barely any hydrogen refueling infrastructure in place, and now a Hyundai executive has revealed that people don’t really want to buy a hydrogen car in the first place.

“The biggest thing is you’ve got to find customers, said Scott Nargar, Senior Manager of Future Mobility & Government Relations at Hyundai Australia, for CarExpert. Despite having problems finding buyers, the Hyundai representative insisted that hydrogen isn’t “dead for passenger vehicles.”

Besides having extremely limited access to refueling stations, hydrogen-powered cars are also more expensive than comparable gas and electric vehicles. That’s not exactly a good look, especially now when prices of new EVs are considerably lower than a decade ago, making them a perfect fit for those who are prepared to make the switch to electric.

What’s more, the electric charging infrastructure is now very well laid out, with even more chargers coming in the near future, making range anxiety and charging anxiety a thing of the past.

So with such easy access to electric cars, why would any company still bother to invest in hydrogen fuel cell vehicles? It all has to do with diversifying. In spite of the huge costs associated with developing a new fuel cell stack and installing refueling stations, some automakers, including Hyundai, believe that hydrogen will still have a place in the future where gas and diesel might not be as ubiquitous as they are today.

While Toyota decided to let anyone in California spend their hard-earned money to buy a Mirai, Hyundai’s hydrogen-fueled dream has been largely limited to a few real-world trials. Its latest passenger FCEV, the second-generation Nexo crossover, can drive roughly 435 miles on a full tank of hydrogen, powered by a 110-kilowatt electric motor and a 2.64-kilowatt-hour high-voltage battery that acts as a buffer between the motor and hydrogen fuel stack.

On face value, the Specialty Equipment Market Association doesn’t sound like much, but if you say it as SEMA, that’s when it catches the attention of enthusiasts. For over 40 years, the SEMA show has showcased some of the latest aftermarket parts, but also showcased some of the best builds and has become a platform for automakers to let their hair down a bit. This year is no exception, of course.

A good number of carmakers have joined the show. Nissan is one of the many, and it has brought three builds for the occasion. There’s the Frontier Ronin Concept, the Armada Jungle Patrol Concept, and the Pathfinder XE-V6 Concept. There’s a good number to cover, so we’ll kick things off with the Pathfinder.

The Nissan Pathfinder changed quite a lot over the years. It started as a Hardbody pickup-based SUV in the ’80s, then became a unibody in the ’90s that still retained truck suspension. After that, it reverted to a truck-based SUV in the 2000s, this time being based on the Frontier, and now, it’s a crossover.

The current Pathfinder is a decent choice in its class, but we wouldn’t really call it an off-roader by any means. Sure, there’s the Rock Creek Edition, but the trim gives more traction on the rough stuff thanks to all-terrains, and nothing really more. It’s a far cry from the D21 from over 40 years ago, having a completely different set of priorities.

Still, that didn’t stop Nissan from looking back to build a special one-off model. Simply called the XE-V6, it nods to one of the slightly lower trims of the original Pathfinder. While that sounds odd, the XE-V6 was the no-nonsense trim that had enough creature comforts at the time but still retained its ruggedness for not much money.

The most obvious change that’s been done to it is the suspension. It’s a four-inch lift kit that’s a custom job, while spacers allow the chunky mud-terrain tires to poke out of the body that little bit more. The front and rear bumpers are a custom job, too, along with the rock sliders.

While no longer a frame-based SUV, the XE-V6 moniker still applies somewhat, as the current Pathfinder still sports a V6 engine. That said, it’s been left untouched, but it has a prototype NISMO cat-back exhaust system. No off-roader build would be complete without the accessories that come along with it, so there are driving lights and a roof rack, plus a spare tire carrier, winch, and underbody protection.

The original XE-V6 was offered with a graphics package, and that’s what this SEMA build tries to capture. Those old enough to remember will recall those stickers on the sides of some Pathfinders, and Nissan did a good job bringing it to the 2020s.

It’s pretty neat that Nissan finds ways to introduce more fun concepts, but we can’t help but wonder about the future Frontier-based Pathfinder that’s coming soon. We’re not saying that this concept isn’t cool, but our brains imagine an even more rugged and squared-off SUV with such upgrades fitted.

Perhaps it’s a preview of what we can expect from the truck-based Pathfinder and Xterra in terms of customization. That said, those models are still a few years away, but if Nissan is whetting our appetites for those SUVs as early as now, consider us excited.

#4433. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

With a long-travel suspension and turbos from the R35 GT-R, this heavily modded mid-size truck is a hardcore desert runner.

In true SEMA fashion, Nissan’s aim for the Frontier Ronin concept was to create an “unstoppable off-road truck.” To that end, the automaker stretched the limits of the Frontier platform’s performance in terms of both the truck’s powertrain and off-road capabilities.

The Frontier’s 3.8-liter V-6 is still present under the hood of the Ronin, but Nissan also made a host of notable changes. For starters, the Ronin features forced induction in the form of the R35 Nissan GT-R’s twin-turbo setup, which is mounted in the rear.

The engine is fed air through a set of custom intakes and kept cool thanks to a custom front-mounted intercooler system. The Smart car had a pretty short life in the United States, especially when it comes to the two-door electric model. However, over in Europe, the two-door urban runabout has become something of an icon, and can often be seen in the busy streets of major cities.

Now, though, there’s a new two-door Smart EV, which harks back to the original ForTwo EQ, but significantly improves on its predecessor’s spec sheet. And to the company’s surprise, the first batch of the new Smart #2 is also proving quite successful, with order books already full.

I’m talking about the limited-run Smart #2 Couture Edition, which kicked off sales of the diminutive EV in Europe. Limited to just 999 units, the two-tone version of the bug-eyed city car is already sold out in all of the countries where it was available, signaling that Europeans are interested in Smart’s modern reinterpretation of the car that started it all.

To be clear, the Smart #2 in its regular trims can still be ordered and probably won’t be sold out anytime soon. But for a car that can only seat two and has a WLTP-rated range of just 180 miles (290 kilometers), it’s a pretty solid start.

The #2 Couture Edition is based on the top Premium trim and comes standard with a glass roof, ambient lighting, heated seats, a heated steering wheel, a Sennheiser audio system, and a wireless charging pad for smartphones. On top of that, the exterior is painted in an exclusive Atelier White Matt color with a Platinum Gold roof. Together with the 16-inch Lyra rims with gold details and suitcase-like straps in the front bumper, the limited edition model is meant to look like the Smart Concept #2 that prefaced the model’s introduction half a year ago.

“Selling out all currently available units of the Smart #2 Couture Edition in just two weeks is an extraordinary achievement,” said Wolfgang Ufer, CEO of Smart Europe GmbH. “And what makes this success even more remarkable is that most of our customers haven't even had the chance to see the car in person yet. For me, this is much more than a sales success. It's a powerful sign of how much people have been waiting for the return of our iconic two-seater.”

The successor to the Smart ForTwo EQ is powered by a 35.8-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, which is almost double the original model’s 17.6-kWh capacity. As a result, the range has also doubled. The charging performance has also been improved dramatically, with the new Smart #2 needing roughly 20 minutes to go from 10% to 80% state of charge.

In several European countries, including Germany, France, and Italy, the new EV starts at €19,990 ($22,500). The first customer deliveries in left-hand drive markets are scheduled for the middle of the second quarter, with right-hand drive markets following in 2027.

#4430. Lincoln Recalls 11,623 SUVs That May Shift Into Neutral While Driving

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

A peculiar fault is causing a major issue for Lincoln’s two premium SUVs.

Nissan Gives the Pathfinder a 4-Inch Lift and Old-School Off-Road Makeover

Ringbrothers Just Made the Ultimate Pontiac GTO

Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol Ditches Roof and Luxury for Serious Off-Roading

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

The automotive industry’s pace is rapid these days. Instead of launching new models every few years, manufacturers are finding ways to refresh, update, or launch cars more quickly to keep buyers interested and capture the market’s short attention span.

While the pace has its benefits, such as a wide variety of up-to-date cars, sometimes it can also lead to production errors. In some cases, these errors start as small, insignificant issues but end up causing much bigger problems. Lincoln’s latest recall advisory represents that very idea: a small fault with big consequences.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) just issued Safety Recall Report 26V688. This report affects the Lincoln brand, specifically the Lincoln Corsair and the Nautilus. In total, the report lists 11,623 affected vehicles, most of which are Nautilus (11,560), with only 63 affected Corsair units. For the Corsair, the affected cars were built from Mar 12, 2026 to Jul 08, 2026, while the Nautilus units were produced from Sep 09, 2025 to Aug 06, 2026.

All NHTSA reports are detailed and sometimes very specific; here is how the report explains the specific issue: “Ford’s team reviewed supplier manufacturing records to determine the population of affected vehicles. Affected vehicles may have been produced with an anti-rust oil that may degrade the conformal coating on the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) of the Integrated Parking Module (IPM). Affected vehicles have HF55 transmissions.

Those who know cars and engineering may already have a sense of how bad the issue is based on the description above. Thankfully, the NHTSA report also has a more layman-friendly explanation: the anti-rust oil could degrade the coating on the PCB, which might cause a drop in voltage for the rotary sensor. If the voltage drops, it could inadvertently shift the car into Neutral while driving, which is a major safety risk. Another issue is that low voltage might also prevent you from shifting out of Park to get going.

According to the report, Ford was not informed by the supplier that the anti-rust oil was changed. Additionally, the new oil didn’t undergo proper validation tests to confirm its compatibility with the part it was applied to. The report also stated that affected cars would be notified through dashboard messages displaying “Service Vehicle Soon” or “Shifting System Error”.

To fix the problem, the Integrated Park Module (IPM) will be replaced with a module that does not contain anti-rust oil that degrades the conformal coating, and the replacement module will be updated with the latest software.

#4428. Tesla Warned Owners Not To Test Emergency Drive Away. Some Did Anyway.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla recently rolled out a new feature that will allow owners to drive away from a Supercharger in an emergency. That feature came with an asterisk that Tesla was abundantly clear about: Don't hit it unless you absolutely need to, or else.

Well, a few owners were curious about what would happen if they decided not to heed that warning and activate the feature while plugged into a Tesla Supercharger. And now, through the magic of social media, we now know exactly what happens when an owner flips the switch.

But first, let's talk about what we know happens when a user tries to activate Emergency Drive Away. The driver first gets a warning that requires them to acknowledge the potential for damage to both their car and the Supercharger. If they choose to hit the Activate button and proceed, the Supercharger will unlock from the charge port so the owner can hit the gas and let the charging handle break away.

Again, this is for an emergency where users need to get away, and get away fast. The cost of damage to the car and the Supercharger are probably worth the owner's safety. That's why Tesla requires that any vehicle which activates Emergency Drive Away visit a Service Center so that the car can be assessed for damage before the warning can be cleared.

One owner who decided to ignore this warning was reportedly hit with a $539 fee for Tesla's service department to inspect their car's charge port. That's despite not actually driving an inch.

Another user on Reddit reported that they wanted to test what would happen "out of curiosity." They tested it in the same way—immediately putting the car in park and not driving an inch before manually pulling the charger out of the car to avoid damaging any of the equipment.

To their surprise, the car displayed an error that could not be cleared except by Tesla service and the Supercharger was pulled out of service. Fortunately, Tesla's service marked their service inspection as "goodwill" and did not charge the driver.

Another owner reported an initial estimate of $255 but ultimately left their service appointment with a $33.15 bill. A different owner was invoiced $178.20 for an inspection following their own curiosity.

Not all tests—whether intentional or not—have been without damage. Another owner on Reddit witnessed a vehicle activate the feature at a public charger and drive away.

The charger stall can be seen flexing from the cable yank and a component hit the ground behind the car, which means that driver may not be as fortunate to receive a no-cost visit to the Service Center as some of the other beta testers have experienced.

The potential bill gets even uglier if Tesla decides to begin charging for potential Supercharger repairs. Costs to the car aside, Tesla says repairing a Supercharger stall damaged by Emergency Drive Away "can be up to $25k."

There is probably room to make activation of this feature harder. But then again, Tesla may not want to make it harder to get away in an emergency. A financial penalty and mandatory post-activation service visit should (in theory) be enough to dissuade owners from activating it when they don't need to. But as we've seen from the above, that might not be the case.

#4426. Toyota’s Corolla Cross EV spotted for the first time [Images]

Toyota is giving its best-selling Corolla a major makeover, and an all-electric version is part of the plan. The upcoming Corolla Cross EV was captured in public for the first time ahead of its expected 2027 debut.

The Corolla has always been “a car for everyone,” Toyota’s former president and current CEO, Koji Sato, said after unveiling the next-gen Corolla Concept at last year’s Japan Mobility Show.

Since it went on sale 60 years ago, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla, making it Toyota’s best-selling vehicle ever.

The Corolla has undergone 12 model changes since 1966, but the compact car is about to undergo its biggest transformation yet.

Although it’s still a top seller, the Corolla has lost some of its appeal as new, more advanced, and efficient options have emerged. Toyota looks to change that with the next-generation model.

It will remain “a car for everyone,” as Sato said, but the next-gen Corolla will come in multiple powertrains, including an all-electric version.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle―whatever the power source―let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive,” Sato said at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Ahead of its expected debut sometime in 2027, a disguised Corolla Cross EV was spotted driving near Toyota’s European headquarters and R&D center.

New images from Chinese media outlet Autohome show what’s expected to be the all-electric Corolla Cross, with a closed-off grille and a unique body design.

The new Corolla will be the first to use Toyota’s new “multipathway” platform that will support electric, hybrid, gas, and other powertrains.

Toyota hasn’t revealed specifics, including battery or powertrain specs, but the next-gen Corolla EV is expected to remain close in style to the Concept. Aside from the massive COROLLA badge on the back, it looks like an entirely different vehicle with a near sports-car-like silhouette.

In an exclusive interview with Japanese media NHK in July, Toyota’s current chairman and former CEO, Akio Toyoda, warned that the company “cannot survive” if it does not adapt amid new competition and technology from China.

During the special, which went behind the scenes at Toyota’s “top secret” development site, several blurred Corolla Concept body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and GR model, were revealed in the background.

According to a recent Nikkei report, Toyota plans to begin production of the next-gen Corolla in 2028 through its joint venture with Chinese state-owned FAW Group, FAW Toyota Motor.

The Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations with a driving range of at least 250 miles.

The hybrid version will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota has yet to confirm the electric version will launch in the US. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

Starting with a 1966 Fastback, they’re marking 125 years of Ford Racing and showing off just how wild you can get with their latest performance parts if you’re building up a classic. This is a project of Ford Customer Service Division, Ford Racing Parts, and Ford Customization.

The bones here are pure 1966 Fastback, so you still get those classic lines everyone loves. But Ford’s given it a meaner look with a black paint job and some loud red and gold touches.

You can’t miss the R125 graphics – big lettering and a bold Ford Racing badge run down the sides. Gold wheels crank up the flash, and the front gets its own R125 makeover. Out back, Ford Racing is splashed across the panel, just in case you forgot what this build is all about.

That fuel injection setup keeps the classic V8 feel but makes the car way more livable for anyone who actually wants to drive it. Ford’s ditched the all-original carburetor setup for something you can easily enjoy owning. Power goes to the wheels through a Tremec TKX-600 five-speed, which is smoother and tougher than the old TKO. Plus, it’s compact enough to fit in builds where you actually care about how the thing drives.

Ford Racing Parts even threw in their trick two-piece valve covers, with swappable tops, O-ring seals, and built-in wire looms – because why not go all out?

The R125 will hit the spotlight at the 2026 SEMA Show for Ford Racing’s big 125th bash. Don’t expect to see it at your local dealer or find a price tag – this one’s all about showing off what you can snag from the Ford Racing Parts catalog.

#4424. Volvo Is Getting Crushed In The U.S.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo is having some trouble adapting to the fast-paced auto market changes in the U.S. From flip-flopping tariffs to the exodus of its sister brand, Polestar, there have been a ton of changes in a relatively short period of time that has been difficult for the Swedes to keep up with.

In its third-quarter earnings call last week, Volvo's leadership admitted that it was struggling to make its endeavors in the U.S. lucrative and that customer optimism in the brand has hit a point not seen in half a century.

"U.S. has proven to be a difficult market to find profitability," said Volvo's Chief Commercial Officer, Erik Severinson, during the company's third quarter earnings call last week. "The consumer sentiment in the U.S. [...] is at a 50-year low."

CEO Hakan Samuelsson said that one of Volvo's oversights was how tariffs would affect its business in the States. He admitted that the company "should have realized" that the tariffs were a real possibility and that they would need to "localize more in the U.S." to address them. The CEO went on to say that Volvo is working to address those tariff-related shortcomings to help strengthen its position in the market.

One of the long-standing ways that Volvo anticipated reversing its sales slump was with the EX60. However, the electric SUV meant to compete with the likes of the BMW iX3 and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric has proven to be a manufacturing challenge. And with EV sales continuing to boom in Europe and other global electrification hotspots, Americans hoping to get an EX60 in their driveway will be waiting longer than originally anticipated while Europe is prioritized.

The CEO also rather publicly addressed the U.S. falling behind of EV adoption.

Without criticizing, Samuelsson noted that Volvo needs to ensure that its offerings in America would address this. Its plant in South Carolina—which is only running at 20% capacity building the Volvo EX90 (and soon the XC60)—is planned for a second new, multi-powertrain vehicle by the top of the decade.

"The U.S. is electrifying slower than the rest of the world. We need to have a new car that is also flexible in that respect, with all-electric, plug-in or hybrid," said Samuelsson.

Volvo is in a tough spot. Like many other automakers, it went all-in on electrification at the same time when other global automakers committed to building all-EV brands. But as the American market reversed course, Volvo pulled what would have otherwise been high-volume BEV vehicles (the EX30 and EX40) for the U.S. market.

The Swedes now recognize that they need to regain traction in one of the world's most important auto markets. That will come through localization to avoid tariffs, and a push for demand through multiple powertrains. Will it work? Well, that's to be seen.

#4422. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

I'd love to have a hot water driven radiant heat system paired with solar and battery storage and a smart management system. Unfortunately, the US seems to lag behind on this, but my sense is that even in Europe the integration between all the components isn't yet as smooth as would be desired.

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4420. BMW's Tesla FSD Rival Hits City Streets In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW's advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is already pretty good and can smoothly cruise highways hands-free. However, BMW wants to up its ADAS game even further by expanding the system to include city driving in 2027. In other words, BMW's rival to Tesla Full Self-Driving (Supervised) is coming soon.

The navigation-guided, "partially automated" system will be able to use BMW maps to make turns, lane changes, navigate roundabouts, and even understand right-of-way situations, BMW announced on Monday. It can already handle some stop-and-go situations, and even stop for traffic lights, but this will be another step up.

"By extending partially automated driving functions to urban areas, we will offer our customers a real improvement in driving comfort—with confident driver assistance in true BMW style," said BMW board member Joachim Post in a statement. "The system will support them seamlessly along the navigation route, from motorways through country roads and into the city."

Much of the auto industry is racing to match Tesla's FSD with their own point-to-point driving systems for cities. Perhaps most importantly, BMW's perennial rival Mercedes-Benz is working on the technology with both Nvidia and Wayve. Rivian plans to launch an in-house point-to-point system to its cars next year.

BMW drivers will be able to see what the car is planning to do in BMW's Panoramic Vision dashboard. The screen in front of the driver will indicate the traffic it's seeing around itself, what it's currently doing, and all other relevant info. Since this is a Level 2 system, drivers will have to remain attentive.

Rollout for this new ADAS will start in Germany next year, with other markets following over time. (BMW didn't announce a timeline for a U.S. rollout.) The hardware for this new ADAS will be standard on several new models, like the BMW iX3, iX4, 3 Series, X5, and 7 Series. The software itself will be available via an over-the-air update, BMW says.
